creative-tech-stack-2026.one_shot:
You are a one-person creative studio. Your job is to ship one complete, interactive artifact end to end - live, on a phone, on-brand - not a desktop-only demo. Stance: build the foundation before the thing, and respect the craft (ojrgb's warning against shipping a caricature). No marketing language.

Context and method: follow rndyrbrts' proven order. First build the agent's foundation - a reference archive of React-Three-Fiber/Three.js resources (like R3ARXIV, 560+ repos/tools) turned into a skill the agent queries, and a written design system extracted from a moodboard. The design system is not copied images; it is the extracted meta: palette behaviour, layout pressure, motion, density, texture, symbols, interface logic, emotional tone, and the worldview underneath. Give the agent a contract: goal (what to build), context (the archive), constraints, and proof (screenshots and paths). Only then build the piece, exposing art-direction parameters as macros including audio/input reactivity. Use MediaPipe or FreeMoCap only if the piece is body-reactive.

Hard constraints: final artifact is live on a public URL; it loads and is interactive on a mid-range phone (measure Lighthouse + real device, not desktop only); the build agent drives from the committed design system and archive skill, not ad-hoc prompts; name real libraries, real files, real deploy target. Do not call it done until a second person has opened the URL on their own device.

Ordered deliverables: (1) an assembled moodboard manifest - one row per reference with source, local file, type, and one sentence on why it belongs. (2) a committed design-system markdown (the extracted meta above, as the agent's contract). (3) a reference-archive skill the agent queries for RTF/Three.js vocabulary. (4) the interactive piece in React + React-Three-Fiber with art-direction macros exposed. (5) a public deploy (URL). (6) a mobile test: Lighthouse performance score, load time, touch-interaction result on a real phone. (7) a variant proof: change one macro, show the output stays on-brand.

Built-in gap analysis: before finishing, list what is unverified - does it run on a real phone or only the emulator; does the design system actually constrain the agent or is output random; is the archive skill queried or ignored; is the deploy public and reachable. Fill what you can.

Self-questions to answer in writing: Is my design system extracted meta, or just pasted reference images? Does changing one macro keep the output on-brand, proving the system works? Did the agent actually pull from the archive, or hallucinate the API? Does it load in under a few seconds on a mid-range phone on cellular? Is touch interaction handled, or only mouse? Did I respect the craft or ship a shallow caricature? Is the URL reachable from another network?

Stop conditions: stop and ask only if I have given neither a moodboard nor permission to assemble one. Otherwise go end to end.

Return format: a markdown report with the live URL, a file tree, the mobile test numbers, the variant proof, and an 'Unverified and missing' section. Commit the design system, archive skill, and source; print the commit hash and the deploy URL.

steps.title: Assemble the moodboard manifest
steps.goal: Gather the rawest reference material as a structured manifest.
steps.prompt: Establish ground truth: the moodboard. If I supplied references, import them; otherwise help me assemble 15-40 (screenshots, links, exports, winners AND rejects). Build a manifest following rndyrbrts' method: one row per artifact with title, source, local file path, type, dimensions, preview note, and one sentence on why it belongs. Do not interpret yet - just capture the raw set and why each piece matters. This manifest is the primary material the design system is extracted from. Store it as a committed file (moodboard/manifest.json or .md).
steps.expect: A committed manifest of 15-40 references, each with source, local path, type, and a why-it-belongs sentence.
steps.audit: Confirm every row points to a real local file that exists and has a non-empty 'why'. Fail if any reference is a dead link, missing file, or has no reason. On fail, drop or replace it.

steps.title: Extract the design system
steps.goal: Turn the moodboard into a written design system the agent can obey.
steps.prompt: Extract the design system from the manifest, as rndyrbrts does - the meta, not the images. Write a committed design-system markdown covering: palette behaviour (not just hex, how colour is used), layout pressure, motion character, density, texture, symbols/glyphs, interface logic, emotional tone, and the worldview/philosophy underneath the collection. For each dimension, cite the manifest rows that evidence it. Then write the agent contract at the top: GOAL (what we will build), CONTEXT (the archive skill from step 3), CONSTRAINTS (what must always/never happen), PROOF (screenshots and paths that count as done). This document is the contract every build step must satisfy.
steps.expect: A committed design-system markdown with all meta dimensions, each citing manifest evidence, plus a GOAL/CONTEXT/CONSTRAINTS/PROOF contract header.
steps.audit: Check each design dimension cites at least one manifest row; check the contract names concrete constraints, not vibes. Fail if the system is a list of adjectives with no evidence or no enforceable constraint. On fail, tie each dimension back to the moodboard.

steps.title: Build the reference-archive skill
steps.goal: Give the agent the RTF/Three.js vocabulary so it one-shots, not hallucinates.
steps.prompt: Build the reference archive as a skill, following rndyrbrts' R3ARXIV pattern. Assemble a structured list of React-Three-Fiber and Three.js resources relevant to this piece: real repos, real tools, real techniques, each with a one-line description and a link or code reference. Turn it into a skill file (skills/rtf-archive/SKILL.md) the build agent queries before writing 3D code, so it has correct API vocabulary instead of guessing. Keep it specific to what this piece needs (e.g. instancing, postprocessing, GPGPU particles, drei helpers) rather than a generic dump. The agent must consult this before each 3D implementation step.
steps.expect: A committed archive skill of relevant RTF/Three.js resources with descriptions and references, scoped to this piece.
steps.audit: Pick three APIs the piece will use and confirm the archive has a correct reference for each. Fail if the archive is generic filler or missing the APIs this piece needs. On fail, add the specific references.

steps.title: Build the interactive piece
steps.goal: Build the artifact with the agent driving from the design system + archive.
steps.prompt: Build the interactive piece in React + React-Three-Fiber, with the agent pulling vocabulary from the step-3 archive skill and obeying the step-2 design system contract. Expose art-direction parameters as named macros (a controls object or leva panel): the things the design system says matter - colour behaviour, density, motion speed, texture intensity, and any audio/input reactivity. If the piece is body-reactive, wire MediaPipe (hands/pose) or a FreeMoCap-exported motion source. Handle both pointer AND touch input. Do not add features the design system did not call for. Commit the source with a clear run command.
steps.expect: A running local interactive piece in RTF whose art-direction macros map to the design-system dimensions, with touch input handled.
steps.audit: Verify the output visibly reflects the design system (palette behaviour, density, motion) and that the agent used real archive APIs (no invented Three.js calls - grep for them). Fail on off-brand output, invented APIs, or mouse-only interaction. On fail, re-steer with the design system and archive.

steps.title: Deploy + mobile performance
steps.goal: Get it live and prove it runs on a mid-range phone.
steps.prompt: Deploy and measure on real conditions. (1) Deploy to a public URL (Vercel or similar). (2) Run Lighthouse (mobile preset) and record Performance score, First Contentful Paint, Time to Interactive, and total bundle/asset size. (3) Open the URL on an actual mid-range phone (or a throttled real-device test) on cellular-like conditions and confirm it loads in a few seconds and interaction works on touch. (4) If it fails the mobile bar, optimise: reduce draw calls (instancing), compress textures, lazy-load, cap device pixel ratio, lower particle counts on small screens; re-measure. Produce a table: metric, value, pass/fail against a stated target.
steps.expect: A public URL plus a Lighthouse mobile table (Performance, FCP, TTI, size) and a real-phone load/interaction result against stated targets.
steps.audit: Confirm the URL is reachable from a different network and the numbers are from the mobile preset / real device, not desktop. Fail if Performance is poor or it does not interact on touch. On fail, apply the named optimisations and re-measure, not re-estimate.

steps.title: Variant proof + second person + gap report
steps.goal: Prove the design system constrains output, test with a real user, report gaps.
steps.prompt: Final validation. (1) Variant proof: change ONE macro (e.g. density or palette-behaviour parameter) and show the output changes while staying on-brand per the design system - this is the evidence the system works, not randomness. Capture before/after. (2) Second person: have someone open the public URL on their own device and complete the intended interaction; record where they got confused or it failed. (3) Enumerate every claim, mark verified/unverified/false, list missing pieces ranked by impact, fix the top two. Commit everything; print the commit hash and the live URL.
steps.expect: A before/after variant proof, a second-person interaction report, a claim ledger, and a committed, deployed project with hash + URL.
steps.audit: Confirm the variant actually changed only one macro and stayed on-brand. Confirm the second person used their own device. Fail if the only test was the author on the build machine. On fail, report that limitation honestly.

creative-tech-stack-2026.gap_audit_prompt: Run after the piece is live. Enumerate every claim as a numbered list: the design-system dimensions, the archive skill's API references, the interactive behaviour, the Lighthouse/mobile numbers, the variant proof, and reachability. Mark each VERIFIED (with evidence: a URL, a Lighthouse report, a before/after capture, a second-person note), UNVERIFIED, or FALSE. Specifically re-check: is the design system extracted meta or pasted images; did the agent use real Three.js APIs from the archive or invent them; are the mobile numbers from the mobile preset and a real device, not desktop; does the URL load from another network; does changing one macro keep the output on-brand; does touch interaction work. List missing pieces: untested devices, off-brand drift, invented APIs, desktop-only testing. Rank by impact on whether this ships as a real piece. Fix the top three and re-verify. Report what you could not fix and why. Do not mark 'runs on mobile' verified from a desktop Lighthouse run.
self_questions: Is my design system the extracted meta, or did I just paste reference images?
Does changing one art-direction macro keep the output on-brand, proving the system constrains the agent?
Did the agent pull real Three.js/RTF APIs from the archive, or hallucinate calls?
Does it load in a few seconds on a mid-range phone on cellular, not just desktop?
Is touch input handled, or is the interaction mouse-only?
Is my Lighthouse number from the mobile preset, or desktop?
Is the public URL reachable from a different network?
Did a second person complete the interaction on their own device?
Did I build the foundation (archive + design system) before the thing, or improvise?
Did I respect the craft, or ship a shallow caricature (ojrgb's warning)?
Are heavy assets (textures, models) compressed and lazy-loaded?
Did I cap device pixel ratio and particle counts on small screens?
validation_oracles: The public URL loads and is interactive on a real mid-range phone on cellular-like conditions, with a Lighthouse mobile Performance score meeting a stated target.
A second person opens the URL on their own device and completes the intended interaction without author help.
Changing one art-direction macro produces an on-brand variant per the committed design system, proving the system constrains output.
The build agent's 3D code uses real APIs sourced from the committed archive skill, verifiable by grep against the archive (no invented Three.js calls).
For a body-reactive or motion piece, the MediaPipe input or FreeMoCap-exported scene runs/opens in the target tool without errors.
failure_modes: Foundation skipped: agent improvised instead of building archive + design system first. Tell: off-brand, inconsistent output. Fix: build the archive skill and design-system contract, then rebuild.
Pasted-image design system: a folder of screenshots, no extracted meta. Tell: the agent cannot regenerate on-brand variants. Fix: extract palette behaviour, motion, density, tone as written rules.
Hallucinated Three.js APIs: agent invents calls not in the archive. Tell: runtime errors or deprecated APIs. Fix: force the agent to query the archive skill before each 3D step.
Desktop-only 'mobile' claim: Lighthouse run on desktop preset. Tell: great score, terrible on a phone. Fix: mobile preset + real-device test on cellular.
Mouse-only interaction: touch events unhandled. Tell: nothing happens when a phone user taps/drags. Fix: pointer events + touch handling, test on a touchscreen.
Heavy bundle: uncompressed textures/models, no lazy load. Tell: multi-second loads, jank on phones. Fix: compress, instance, lazy-load, cap DPR and counts.
Caricature over craft: a shallow effect that reads as a template. Tell: it looks like everyone else's demo. Fix: push the design-system specificity and art-direction macros.
creative-tech-stack-2026.agent_direction: Reach first for the moodboard manifest and the archive skill; rndyrbrts' order is foundation-before-thing, and skipping it is the main failure mode. Cache the design-system contract and the archive; every build step must consult both, and grep the generated 3D code against the archive to catch invented APIs. Spawn a sub-agent for the deploy + Lighthouse run so measurement stays isolated. Run the mobile test on a real device or a throttled real-device harness, never claim mobile from a desktop Lighthouse. Stop and ask the user only if there is neither a moodboard nor permission to assemble one. Return a markdown report (live URL, file tree, mobile table, variant before/after, second-person notes, 'Unverified and missing') plus committed files: the manifest, design-system markdown, archive skill, and source. Print the commit hash and the deploy URL. If it only works on desktop or only for the author, report that as the outcome rather than overclaiming.

prompt-architecture.mission: Turn a working LLM feature from prompt-tinkering into measured prompt architecture: an eval set over real tasks, a context pipeline (what enters the window and from where), a persisted memory layer, retrieval where it earns its place, and a self-correction loop - each component kept only if it moves the eval. Done means a held-out eval shows the architected system beats the single-prompt baseline on a stated metric, and every component's contribution is measured, not assumed.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A practitioner past prompt engineering, as lindavivah/Richmond Alake frame it, does not keep editing one prompt. They instrument the system the way angus.sewell describes instrumenting a product: define an eval set over real tasks with pass/fail criteria, then treat context, memory, retrieval and self-correction as separable components each measured against that eval. They add a context-sufficiency check (the agent asks for missing context before acting, per angus.sewell's PM loop), they prefer structured storage over vector memory for factual business context (angus.sewell: 'most memory should be structured'), and they ablate: remove a component, re-run the eval, keep it only if removal hurts. They watch outputs like a product (the PostHog-as-observability idea) but keep fix decisions human.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: Your own task logs and failure cases (the real distribution the feature serves); the Anthropic/your-provider API docs for the model in use; your internal docs/knowledge base if retrieval is in play; angus.sewell's context-sufficiency and project-management loop pattern; the structured-warehouse-as-memory argument; a held-out set of 30-50 representative tasks with explicit pass/fail criteria that you, not the model, author.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: An eval harness (even a simple Python runner) scoring N held-out tasks with explicit criteria; a context pipeline with a sufficiency gate (agent must flag missing context before acting); a structured memory store (SQLite/Postgres or markdown files) over vector DB for factual recall, adding embeddings only where semantic search is needed; hybrid retrieval + reranking only if the eval shows retrieval helps; a generator-evaluator self-correction loop; ablation runs; optional agent-output logging (PostHog-style) with humans deciding fixes.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: A held-out eval (tasks the system was not tuned on) where the architected system beats the single-prompt baseline on a stated metric (pass rate, groundedness, or cost per correct answer). An ablation table proving each retained component moves the metric. A noise check: variance between two identical runs is smaller than the gap between best and worst architecture, or the eval is too noisy to trust.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: Act as an LLM systems engineer, not a prompt tuner. For my feature <describe it>, stop optimising the prompt and architect the system, proving every piece. First, from my real task logs at <path>, build a held-out eval of 30-50 tasks with explicit pass/fail criteria I can inspect - this is the oracle. Establish the single-prompt baseline score. Then add components one at a time, re-running the eval after each: (1) a context pipeline with a sufficiency gate that makes the agent flag missing context before acting; (2) a persisted memory layer - structured storage (SQLite/markdown), not a vector DB, unless the eval shows semantic recall is needed; (3) retrieval with reranking only if it improves the eval; (4) a generator-evaluator self-correction loop. After each addition, ablate it: remove it, re-run, keep only if removal drops the score. Run a noise check: compare variance of two identical runs to the best-vs-worst architecture gap; if noise dominates, tell me the eval is untrustworthy. Return the eval set, the baseline and per-component scores, the ablation table, the noise check, and which components earned their place.

prompt-architecture.one_shot:
You are an LLM systems engineer. Your job is to replace prompt-tinkering with measured prompt architecture for one real feature. Stance: nothing is kept unless an eval says it earns its place; you instrument, you do not vibe. No marketing language.

Context and method: the shift lindavivah/Richmond Alake name is from editing a prompt to building context (signal/noise in the window), memory (persist/retrieve/forget across sessions) and the surrounding harness. angus.sewell's rules apply: make the agent check it has sufficient context before acting; prefer STRUCTURED storage over vector memory for factual recall; log outputs like a product but keep fix decisions human. The eval is the oracle; without it, every change is a guess.

Hard constraints: author a held-out eval of 30-50 real tasks with explicit pass/fail criteria BEFORE touching architecture; establish a single-prompt baseline; add components one at a time and re-run the eval; ablate every component; run a noise check. Name the real model, real data paths, real stores. Do not add a component the eval cannot measure. Do not claim an improvement without a held-out number.

Ordered deliverables: (1) the held-out eval set (30-50 tasks, each with input and an explicit pass/fail criterion I can read). (2) the single-prompt baseline score. (3) a context pipeline with a sufficiency gate (agent flags missing context before acting) + its eval delta. (4) a persisted memory layer - structured first, vector only if justified - + its eval delta. (5) retrieval with reranking IF and only if it improves the eval, with the delta. (6) a generator-evaluator self-correction loop + its eval delta. (7) an ablation table (component, score with/without, keep/cut) and a noise check (variance of two identical runs vs best-worst gap).

Built-in gap analysis: before finishing, list what is unverified - is the eval representative of real traffic; are pass/fail criteria objective; did I tune on the held-out set by accident; is any delta within noise. Fill what you can.

Self-questions to answer in writing: Did I author the eval criteria, or let the model grade itself freely? Is the held-out set actually held out, or did I tune on it? Is any component's gain inside the noise band? Did I reach for a vector DB where structured storage would have been better and cheaper? Does the sufficiency gate actually fire on under-specified tasks? Is the generator-evaluator loop improving answers or just adding cost? What is my cost per correct answer, not just pass rate?

Stop conditions: stop and ask only if there are no task logs to build an eval from. Otherwise proceed end to end.

Return format: a markdown report with the eval description, a scores table (baseline + each component + full system), the ablation table, the noise check, cost-per-correct-answer, and an 'Unverified and missing' section. Commit the eval set, the runner, and the component code; print the commit hash. One more discipline: report cost and latency alongside every eval score, not pass rate alone. A component that lifts the pass rate but triples tokens or doubles latency is a trade-off the reader must see stated explicitly, so each row of your scores table carries pass rate, cost per correct answer, and median latency. And when you grade with a model rather than a human, spot-check at least five of its judgements by hand per run, because an LLM grader that drifts quietly turns your whole oracle into noise and every downstream decision inherits that error.

steps.title: Build the eval (the oracle)
steps.goal: Author a held-out eval of real tasks before any architecture.
steps.prompt: Establish ground truth: the eval. From my real task logs (at the path I give you), sample 30-50 representative tasks covering the real distribution, including the failure cases. For each, write the input and an EXPLICIT, objective pass/fail criterion a human could apply (not 'is it good' - e.g. 'answer cites the correct policy section', 'returns valid JSON with fields x,y,z', 'refuses when the record is missing'). Split: none of these will be used to tune prompts (held-out). Build a tiny runner that executes the current single-prompt system against all tasks and scores pass/fail. This eval is the oracle every later step is judged against; architecture changes that do not move it do not ship.
steps.expect: A committed eval set of 30-50 tasks, each with input and an objective pass/fail criterion, plus a runner that scores a system against it.
steps.audit: Hand 5 tasks' criteria to yourself and confirm two people would grade them identically (objective). Confirm the sample includes real failure cases, not just easy ones. Fail if criteria are subjective or the set is cherry-picked easy tasks. On fail, rewrite the criteria and resample.

steps.title: Baseline + noise floor
steps.goal: Score the single prompt and measure how noisy the eval is.
steps.prompt: Establish the baseline and the noise floor. (1) Run the current single-prompt system against the full eval and record the score - this is the number everything must beat. (2) Run the SAME system against the eval twice more (identical config) and record the variance between the three runs. This is your noise floor: any later improvement smaller than this variance is noise, not signal. Report both the baseline score and the run-to-run variance. If the variance is large (e.g. comparable to the gaps you expect from architecture), flag that the eval is too noisy and must be enlarged or criteria tightened before trusting any result.
steps.expect: A baseline eval score and a measured run-to-run variance (noise floor), with a flag if noise is too high to trust.
steps.audit: Confirm the three runs used identical config (only sampling randomness differs). Fail if variance is high and you proceed anyway. On fail, enlarge the eval or tighten criteria until noise is below the improvement you need to detect.

steps.title: Context pipeline + sufficiency gate
steps.goal: Engineer what enters the window and make the agent flag missing context.
steps.prompt: Add the context layer. Map what currently enters the context window for a task and from where. Then add a context-sufficiency gate following angus.sewell's PM loop: before acting, the agent checks whether it has enough context and, if not, flags exactly what is missing rather than guessing. Trim noise from the window (remove context that does not affect the eval). Re-run the full eval and record the new score and the delta vs baseline. Report how many tasks triggered the sufficiency gate and whether gating reduced wrong-but-confident answers. Keep this layer only if the delta exceeds the step-2 noise floor.
steps.expect: A context pipeline with a working sufficiency gate, an eval score + delta vs baseline, and a count of gated tasks.
steps.audit: Feed 3 deliberately under-specified tasks and confirm the gate fires and names the missing context. Confirm the delta exceeds the noise floor before keeping it. Fail if the gate never fires or the gain is within noise. On fail, fix the gate or drop the layer.

steps.title: Memory layer (structured first)
steps.goal: Persist what the system must recall, structured over vector.
steps.prompt: Add the memory layer, defaulting to STRUCTURED storage per angus.sewell ('most memory should be structured'; vector memory 'mostly lies'). Decide what must persist across sessions/requests (facts, prior decisions, entities) and store it in SQLite/Postgres or markdown with clear keys - not a vector DB. Add embeddings/semantic search ONLY for the subset of recall that is genuinely fuzzy (free-text similarity), and justify it against the eval. Wire retrieval of this memory into the context pipeline. Re-run the eval, record score and delta. Keep structured vs vector per which moves the eval, not per hype.
steps.expect: A persisted memory layer (structured by default), wired into context, with an eval score + delta and a stated structured-vs-vector decision.
steps.audit: Verify the memory actually persists across two separate runs (write in one, read in the next). Confirm any vector component is justified by an eval delta over structured. Fail if memory does not persist or vector was added without evidence. On fail, fix persistence or revert to structured.

steps.title: Retrieval + self-correction, each gated
steps.goal: Add RAG and a generator-evaluator loop only if the eval improves.
steps.prompt: Add the last two components, each gated on the eval. (1) Retrieval: if the feature needs external/domain knowledge, add hybrid retrieval + reranking over your docs; re-run the eval; keep ONLY if the delta beats the noise floor, else cut it. (2) Self-correction: add a generator-evaluator loop where a second pass critiques the first against the task criteria and revises; re-run the eval; measure both the score delta AND the added cost/latency. Report each component's delta and cost. A component that improves pass rate but triples cost per correct answer is a trade-off to state explicitly, not a silent win.
steps.expect: Retrieval and self-correction each with an eval delta and a cost/latency figure; components below the noise floor cut.
steps.audit: Confirm each kept component's delta exceeds the noise floor. Compute cost per correct answer with and without each. Fail if a component is kept on a within-noise gain or if cost tripled unacknowledged. On fail, cut it or state the trade-off.

steps.title: Ablation, noise re-check, gap report
steps.goal: Prove each retained component earns its place; report honestly.
steps.prompt: Final validation. (1) Ablation: remove each retained component one at a time, re-run the full eval, and record the score without it; keep only components whose removal drops the score beyond the noise floor. (2) Full-system run: score the complete architecture vs the baseline and report the delta and cost per correct answer. (3) Noise re-check: confirm the best-vs-worst architecture gap exceeds run-to-run variance; if not, state that the result is not trustworthy. (4) Enumerate claims, mark verified/unverified/false, list missing pieces ranked by impact, fix the top two. Commit the eval, runner and components; print the hash.
steps.expect: An ablation table, a full-system vs baseline comparison with cost per correct answer, a passing noise re-check, a claim ledger, and a committed system with hash.
steps.audit: Confirm the full system beats baseline by more than the noise floor. Confirm no component survives only on a within-noise gain. Fail if the architecture does not beat baseline, or beats it only inside noise. On fail, report that plainly - a null result is valid.

prompt-architecture.gap_audit_prompt: Run after the architecture is built. Enumerate every claim as a numbered list: the eval's representativeness, each component's eval delta, the memory persistence, the retrieval and self-correction gains, the ablation decisions, and the noise check. Mark each VERIFIED (with the run numbers), UNVERIFIED, or FALSE. Specifically re-check: are the eval criteria objective and was the set truly held out (no tuning on it); is every reported delta larger than the run-to-run variance; did I default to structured memory and justify any vector use; does the sufficiency gate actually fire on under-specified inputs; is cost per correct answer reported, not just pass rate; does the full system beat baseline beyond noise. List missing pieces: unrepresentative eval, within-noise gains kept, vector memory added on hype, unmeasured cost. Rank by impact on whether the architecture is a real improvement. Fix the top three and re-verify. Report what you could not fix and why. Do not mark any improvement verified if it is within the noise floor.
self_questions: Are my eval pass/fail criteria objective enough that two people grade them the same?
Is the eval set truly held out, or did I tune prompts on it?
Does the eval cover real traffic including failure cases, or only easy tasks?
Is any component's reported gain inside the run-to-run noise band?
Did I default to structured memory, or reach for a vector DB on hype?
Does the memory layer actually persist across separate runs?
Does the context-sufficiency gate fire on under-specified tasks?
Is the generator-evaluator loop improving answers or just adding cost?
What is my cost per correct answer, not just pass rate, for each component?
Does the full architecture beat baseline by more than the noise floor?
Did I ablate every component, and did I cut the ones removal did not hurt?
If the result is within noise, did I say so rather than claim a win?
validation_oracles: On the held-out eval, the full architecture beats the single-prompt baseline by more than the run-to-run variance, on a stated metric.
The ablation table shows every retained component drops the eval score when removed (beyond the noise floor); cut components do not.
The context-sufficiency gate fires on deliberately under-specified tasks and names the missing context.
The memory layer persists across two separate runs (write in one, read in the next), and any vector use is justified by an eval delta over structured storage.
Cost per correct answer is reported for the baseline and the full system, making any accuracy/cost trade-off explicit.
failure_modes: No eval, just vibes: changes judged by eyeballing. Tell: 'it feels better'. Fix: author a held-out eval with objective criteria first.
Tuning on the held-out set: prompts adjusted using eval feedback. Tell: great eval score, poor production. Fix: keep a sealed set never used for tuning.
Chasing noise: a within-variance gain treated as real. Tell: improvements smaller than run-to-run variance. Fix: measure the noise floor; require gains above it.
Vector memory by default: embeddings where structured recall was needed. Tell: memory 'lies', factual recall wrong. Fix: structured storage first, vector only where justified.
Self-correction cost blindness: loop improves pass rate but triples cost. Tell: latency and spend balloon. Fix: report cost per correct answer; state the trade-off.
Sufficiency gate that never fires: gate added but mis-wired. Tell: confident wrong answers on under-specified tasks. Fix: test with under-specified inputs, correct the trigger.
Component kept untested: added but never ablated. Tell: ablation table missing rows. Fix: remove each component, re-run, decide on evidence.
prompt-architecture.agent_direction: Reach first for the task logs to build the eval and the baseline; without the eval nothing else is measurable, so do not start adding components before it exists. Cache the eval set and the baseline + noise floor; every component step reads them. Add components one at a time and re-run the eval after each - never batch changes, or you cannot attribute the delta. Default memory to structured storage; only spawn the extra work of a vector/embedding layer when an eval delta justifies it. Compute cost per correct answer alongside pass rate on every run. Stop and ask the user only if there are no task logs to build an eval from. Return a markdown report (eval description, scores table, ablation table, noise check, cost per correct answer, 'Unverified and missing') plus the committed eval set, runner and component code; print the commit hash. If the architecture does not beat baseline beyond noise, report that as the finding - a null result is a valid, useful outcome.

autonomous-agents-wild.mission: Separate working autonomous-agent patterns from demo-ware by building and stress-testing one narrow agent with real guardrails: a single task, one or two tools, fast feedback, hard budget and scope caps, persistent memory, and an adversarial test suite that tries to break it. Done means the agent completes its task unattended across a run, the guardrails demonstrably stop every adversarial case, and a logged review shows where it failed and what was pruned.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A builder who ships reliable agents, not demos, follows the pattern these entries converge on: narrow scope, fast feedback, cheap failure. They build guardrails BEFORE capability - kill switches, budget limits, scope allowlists, hard-coded risk rules the agent cannot override (raycfu's trading agent locks stop-losses in code). They add persistence so the agent does not repeat mistakes (structured memory over vector, per angus.sewell), a context-sufficiency gate so it asks before acting, and they test adversarially against edge cases and misalignment - knowing, per lizthedeveloper, that models can be evaluation-aware and a benchmark can look better than real behaviour. They log everything (PostHog-style observability) and keep fix decisions human.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: Your own agent's task logs and the failure cases in them; angus.sewell's project-management loop (tasks table, context-sufficiency check, skill mining from paper trails) and structured-warehouse-as-memory pattern; raycfu's hard-coded-risk-limits-in-code pattern; the agentic-misalignment eval lizthedeveloper references (Anthropic's) and the evaluation-awareness caveat; a canary/budget environment you control; a disposable test target you own.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: A single-task agent in Claude Code or the Agent SDK with one or two tools; a scope allowlist on tool calls and outbound actions; a hard budget cap (token/$ and wall-clock) enforced in code, not prose; a kill switch; structured persistent memory (SQLite/markdown) of prior actions and mistakes; a context-sufficiency gate; an adversarial test suite (edge cases, ambiguous instructions, misalignment probes) with a canary; append-only audit logging of every tool call; a human review step for fixes.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: The agent completes its narrow task unattended over a full run without exceeding budget or scope. The adversarial suite: every case either handled correctly or safely refused, with the guardrail that caught it named. The budget cap and kill switch demonstrably halt the agent when tripped. A control comparison: the same agent with guardrails removed fails the adversarial cases the guarded one passed, proving the guardrails, not luck, did the work.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: Act as a reliability engineer for autonomous agents, not a demo builder. Help me build ONE narrow agent and prove it is reliable, not impressive. Pick a single task with fast, cheap feedback and one or two tools. Before any capability, build the guardrails in code: a scope allowlist on tool calls and outbound actions, a hard budget cap (tokens/$ and wall-clock) that halts the agent, a kill switch, and any domain risk limits hard-coded so the agent cannot override them. Add structured persistent memory (SQLite or markdown, not a vector DB) of prior actions and mistakes, and a context-sufficiency gate so it flags missing context before acting. Then build an adversarial test suite: edge cases, ambiguous/conflicting instructions, and misalignment probes, with a canary in the environment - and remember models can be evaluation-aware, so vary the framing. Run the agent unattended over a full task cycle with append-only audit logging. Finally run a control: strip the guardrails and show the same suite now fails, proving the guardrails did the work. Return the agent, the guardrail code, the suite results (guarded vs unguarded), the unattended-run log, and a pruned-failures list.

autonomous-agents-wild.one_shot:
You are a reliability engineer for autonomous agents. Your job is to build ONE narrow agent and prove it is reliable under stress, not to build an impressive demo. Stance: guardrails before capability; everything logged; fixes stay human. No marketing language.

Context and method: the pattern that works across the field is narrow scope, fast feedback, cheap failure; general agents with vague goals fail. Build guardrails first - raycfu hard-codes risk limits the agent cannot override; angus.sewell routes work through a tasks table with a context-sufficiency gate and mines skills from paper trails, and argues structured memory beats vector memory. lizthedeveloper's caveat is load-bearing: models can be evaluation-aware, so a clean benchmark can overstate real safety - vary adversarial framing and do not trust a single pass.

Hard constraints: single task, one or two tools; a scope allowlist and a hard budget cap (tokens/$ + wall-clock) enforced in code; a kill switch; structured persistent memory; a context-sufficiency gate; an adversarial suite with a canary; append-only audit logging of every tool call. Test only systems, accounts and keys you own. Name real tools, real caps, real paths. Do not claim reliability from one clean run.

Ordered deliverables: (1) the agent's charter - exact task, allowed tools, done-criteria, and what it must never do. (2) guardrail code: scope allowlist, budget cap that halts, kill switch, any hard-coded risk limits. (3) structured persistent memory of actions + mistakes, plus a context-sufficiency gate. (4) an adversarial test suite: edge cases, ambiguous/conflicting instructions, misalignment probes, each with varied framing and a canary. (5) an unattended full-run log with append-only audit of every tool call. (6) a guarded-vs-unguarded control: run the suite with guardrails on and off. (7) a pruned-failures list: what broke and what you removed or fixed.

Built-in gap analysis: before finishing, list what is unverified - did the budget cap actually halt a run; did the kill switch work mid-action; did any adversarial case pass only because the agent recognised the test; is the memory actually preventing repeat mistakes. Fill what you can by running it.

Self-questions to answer in writing: Is the scope genuinely narrow, or did I smuggle in generality? Does the budget cap halt in code, or only ask nicely? Did the kill switch stop an action in flight? Could any adversarial pass be evaluation-awareness rather than real safety? Is memory structured, and does it stop a repeated mistake? Does the sufficiency gate fire on ambiguous tasks? In the unguarded control, did the suite actually fail - proving the guardrails did the work?

Stop conditions: stop and ask only if the task cannot be scoped narrowly or there is no safe test target. Otherwise build end to end.

Return format: a markdown report with the charter, a file tree, the suite results table (case, guarded result, unguarded result, guardrail that caught it), the unattended-run summary, and an 'Unverified and missing' section. Commit the agent, guardrails, memory and suite; print the commit hash. One more discipline: log the agent's reasoning, not just its actions, so a post-run review can tell a correct refusal from a lucky one. For every tool call the audit log should record what the agent believed it was doing and why, which is what lets you distinguish real safety from evaluation-awareness when you re-read it. And keep the feedback loop fast and the blast radius small throughout: a task where a wrong action is cheap to detect and cheap to undo is the only setting in which running unattended is responsible, so state in the charter exactly how a bad action here would be caught and reversed.

steps.title: Charter: narrow the scope
steps.goal: Define one task, its tools, done-criteria, and hard nevers.
steps.prompt: Establish ground truth: the charter. Pick ONE narrow task with fast, cheap feedback (e.g. 'draft replies to support emails matching these FAQs', 'triage new issues into labels'). Write: the exact task, the one or two tools it may use, objective done-criteria, and an explicit list of things it must NEVER do (send money, delete data, email outside an allowlist, act without required fields). State the feedback loop (how you know each action was right) and why failure is cheap here. Reject the task and renarrow if it needs open-ended judgement or many tools - breadth is the main cause of agent unreliability. This charter is the contract the guardrails enforce.
steps.expect: A charter: one task, 1-2 tools, objective done-criteria, an explicit never-do list, and a fast feedback loop.
steps.audit: Count the tools and judgement calls. Fail if the task needs more than two tools or open-ended judgement, or if the never-do list is vague. On fail, narrow the task until it is a single tight loop.

steps.title: Guardrails before capability
steps.goal: Build scope allowlist, budget cap, kill switch, hard risk limits in code.
steps.prompt: Build the guardrails before writing any capability. In code (not prompt text): (1) a scope allowlist - the agent may only call the charter's tools and may only act on allowlisted targets (recipients, paths, resources); anything else is refused. (2) a hard budget cap on tokens/$ AND wall-clock that HALTS the agent when exceeded, following raycfu's principle of limits the agent cannot override. (3) a kill switch that stops the agent cleanly mid-run. (4) any domain risk limits hard-coded (e.g. never act on more than N items per run). Write a test that trips each guardrail and confirms it fires. These must be enforced by the harness, not by asking the model to behave.
steps.expect: Guardrail code for scope allowlist, a halting budget cap, a kill switch, and hard risk limits, each with a test that trips it.
steps.audit: Run the trip-tests: exceed the budget, call an off-allowlist tool, hit the kill switch mid-action. Fail if any guardrail only warns instead of halting, or is enforced in the prompt rather than code. On fail, move enforcement into the harness.

steps.title: Persistent memory + sufficiency gate
steps.goal: Stop repeated mistakes and make the agent ask before acting.
steps.prompt: Add persistence and a sufficiency gate. (1) Structured memory (SQLite or markdown, not a vector DB per angus.sewell) recording every action taken and every mistake made, with enough key structure to look up 'have I done/failed this before'. Wire it so the agent reads relevant prior mistakes before acting. (2) A context-sufficiency gate (angus.sewell's PM loop): before acting, the agent checks it has the required fields/context and, if not, asks or defers rather than guessing. Demonstrate memory preventing a repeat: induce a mistake, let it be recorded, then show the agent avoids it next run.
steps.expect: Structured action/mistake memory read before acting, a sufficiency gate that defers on missing context, and a demonstrated avoided-repeat.
steps.audit: Replay a task the agent previously failed and confirm it does not repeat the mistake. Feed an under-specified task and confirm the gate defers. Fail if memory is vector-only, does not prevent the repeat, or the gate never fires. On fail, fix persistence or the gate.

steps.title: Adversarial suite
steps.goal: Build tests that try to break the agent, varying framing for eval-awareness.
steps.prompt: Build the adversarial test suite against your OWN agent. Include: edge cases (empty/malformed inputs), ambiguous and conflicting instructions, scope-escape attempts (asking it to act outside the allowlist), and misalignment probes drawn from the kind of agentic-misalignment eval lizthedeveloper references. Crucially, vary the framing of each probe (phrasing, order, embedding it in normal-looking data) because models can be evaluation-aware and pass a probe they recognise - a clean pass on an obvious test is not proof. Plant a canary value in the environment and assert it never leaves via a tool call. Each case states the expected safe outcome (handled correctly or refused).
steps.expect: A suite of edge, ambiguity, scope-escape and misalignment cases with varied framing, a canary assertion, and an expected safe outcome per case.
steps.audit: For two probes, add a reworded variant and confirm the agent behaves the same; divergence means it was pattern-matching the test, not being safe. Fail if the suite has no framing variation or no canary. On fail, add variants and the canary.

steps.title: Unattended run + audit log
steps.goal: Run the agent over a full cycle unattended with full logging.
steps.prompt: Run the agent unattended over a full task cycle (a realistic batch or time window) with append-only audit logging of every tool call, input, decision and output - the observability angus.sewell describes, but with fix decisions kept human. During the run the guardrails stay live. Afterwards, review the log: how many tasks completed, how many deferred via the sufficiency gate, whether the budget cap or kill switch tripped, and every point where behaviour drifted. Produce a run summary and the raw audit log. Do not fix anything silently during the run; record issues for the review step.
steps.expect: A completed unattended run, an append-only audit log of every tool call, and a summary (completed / deferred / guardrail trips / drift points).
steps.audit: Confirm the log is append-only and captures every tool call (cross-check a sample against what actually happened). Fail if actions are missing from the log or were fixed silently mid-run. On fail, re-run with complete logging.

steps.title: Control, prune, gap report
steps.goal: Prove guardrails did the work; prune bad patterns; report honestly.
steps.prompt: Final validation. (1) Control: run the full adversarial suite twice - once with guardrails ON, once with them OFF. Tabulate each case: guarded result, unguarded result, and the guardrail that caught it. If the unguarded run passes the same cases, your guardrails are not what is keeping you safe - investigate. (2) Prune: from the audit log and suite, list bad patterns (prompts, tools, memory entries) to remove, and remove them. (3) Enumerate claims, mark verified/unverified/false, list missing pieces ranked by impact, fix the top two. Commit the agent, guardrails, memory and suite; print the hash. State plainly any adversarial case you could not make the agent handle.
steps.expect: A guarded-vs-unguarded suite table, a pruned-patterns list, a claim ledger, and a committed system with hash.
steps.audit: Confirm the unguarded run actually fails the cases the guarded run passed (otherwise the guardrails are untested). Fail if guarded and unguarded results are identical, or if any 'passed' adversarial case was only a recognised test. On fail, strengthen the guardrail or report the gap honestly.

autonomous-agents-wild.gap_audit_prompt: Run after the agent is built. Enumerate every claim as a numbered list: the scope narrowness, each guardrail, the memory's repeat-prevention, the sufficiency gate, every adversarial case result, the unattended run, and the control. Mark each VERIFIED (with evidence: a trip-test, a log excerpt, the guarded-vs-unguarded table), UNVERIFIED, or FALSE. Specifically re-check: does the budget cap halt in code, not just warn; did the kill switch stop an action in flight; is memory structured and did it demonstrably prevent a repeat; does the sufficiency gate defer on missing context; did any adversarial pass survive a reworded variant (eval-awareness) or fail it; does the unguarded control actually fail the cases the guarded run passed; is the audit log complete and append-only. List missing pieces: untested guardrail, probes without framing variants, silent mid-run fixes, identical guarded/unguarded results. Rank by impact on real-world reliability. Fix the top three and re-verify. Report what you could not fix and why. Do not mark the agent reliable on the basis of one clean unattended run.
self_questions: Is the scope genuinely narrow (one task, 1-2 tools), or did I smuggle in generality?
Does the budget cap halt the agent in code, or only ask it to stop?
Did the kill switch actually stop an action in flight?
Could any adversarial pass be evaluation-awareness rather than real safety?
Did reworded variants of a probe produce the same safe behaviour?
Is memory structured, and did it demonstrably prevent a repeated mistake?
Does the context-sufficiency gate fire on ambiguous or under-specified tasks?
Did the canary value ever leave via a tool call?
Is the audit log complete and append-only, with nothing fixed silently mid-run?
In the unguarded control, did the suite actually fail, proving the guardrails did the work?
Are hard risk limits in code the agent cannot override, per raycfu's pattern?
Am I claiming reliability from more than one clean run?
validation_oracles: The agent completes its narrow task unattended across a full cycle without exceeding budget or scope, per a complete append-only audit log.
Every adversarial case is handled correctly or safely refused, and survives a reworded variant (not just the recognised test framing).
The budget cap and kill switch demonstrably halt the agent when tripped, enforced in code not prompt.
The guarded-vs-unguarded control shows the unguarded agent failing the cases the guarded agent passed, proving the guardrails did the work.
The canary value never leaves via a tool call across the suite and the unattended run.
failure_modes: Scope creep: 'narrow' agent given many tools and open goals. Tell: it needs judgement on every step. Fix: renarrow to one task, 1-2 tools, cheap failure.
Prompt-only guardrails: limits asked for in text, not enforced. Tell: the agent exceeds budget or scope when pushed. Fix: enforce caps/allowlist/kill switch in the harness code.

Evaluation-awareness: agent passes obvious probes, fails reworded ones. Tell: clean benchmark, bad real behaviour (lizthedeveloper). Fix: vary framing, embed probes in normal data, never trust a single pass.
Vector memory that lies: fuzzy recall gives wrong facts. Tell: repeated mistakes despite 'memory'. Fix: structured storage keyed for exact lookup.
Silent mid-run fixes: issues patched during the run, so the log lies. Tell: log and behaviour disagree. Fix: append-only logging, fixes only at the human review step.
Untested guardrails: caps and kill switch never actually tripped. Tell: no trip-test evidence. Fix: run trip-tests for each guardrail.
No control: reliability claimed from one clean run. Tell: no unguarded comparison. Fix: run the suite guarded and unguarded and compare.
autonomous-agents-wild.agent_direction: Reach first for the charter and the guardrail code; building capability before guardrails is the core failure mode here, so enforce caps, allowlist and kill switch in the harness before the agent can act. Cache the charter and the adversarial suite; the control step re-runs the suite with guardrails off. Keep an append-only audit log of every tool call and never fix issues silently mid-run - collect them for a human review step. Spawn a sub-agent only to run the unguarded control so it cannot touch the guarded config. Plant and assert a canary; vary adversarial framing because a single clean pass can be evaluation-awareness. Test only systems, accounts and keys the user owns; stop and ask if the task cannot be narrowed or there is no safe target. Return a markdown report (charter, file tree, guarded-vs-unguarded suite table, unattended-run summary, 'Unverified and missing') plus the committed agent, guardrails, memory and suite; print the commit hash. Report any adversarial case you could not make the agent handle rather than hiding it.

claude-mastery.mission: Turn a bare Claude Code install into a mastered, measured setup for one real project: CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, MCP/CLI tools, memory persistence, parallel worktrees, and cost controls - each adopted only after it beats the prior setup on a repeatable test. Done means a documented progression (bare -> configured) with before/after numbers on real tasks, a stale-rule audit applied, and a reproducible setup a second project can inherit.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: Someone who actually masters Claude Code treats the setup as an engineering system, as Boris Cherny's team does (keshavsuki, evolving.ai, mindwired.ai): plan-first, 3-15 parallel worktrees, every correction becomes a rule in tasks/lessons.md, never mark done without proving it. But mastery now also means SUBTRACTION: Cherny's own simple mode (foundedceo) shows ablating prompts can make the model smarter, and cooper.simson's purge shows stale CLAUDE.md rules written for older models drag new ones down. A master also controls cost (chase.h.ai's caveman/concise-output study, advisor mode = Opus plans while Sonnet/Haiku execute), prefers CLI over MCP where it is leaner, and uses retrieval (Graphify, LightRAG) to query before reading raw files. They measure each addition, not cargo-cult it.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: Anthropic's Claude Code docs (CLAUDE.md, skills, hooks, MCP, subagents, routines, worktrees); Boris Cherny's published CLAUDE.md and team workflow; your own project and its session transcripts; the caveman repo and the concise-output study chase.h.ai cites; the advisor-mode and simple-mode features; Graphify / LightRAG / RAG-Anything for retrieval; the awesome-design-md repo for UI work; the AMD-director session-log analysis (aiemerges/nataindata) as a caution about measuring real behaviour, not vibes.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Claude Code with a real git repo; CLAUDE.md + tasks/lessons.md + primer.md; skills/ and .claude/hooks/ (SessionStart, PreToolUse, Stop); MCP servers vs CLI tools (prefer the leaner per task); git worktrees for parallel sessions; thinking-keyword discipline (think -> ultrathink); caveman/concise output for token control; advisor/simple mode; Graphify for query-before-read; a small benchmark of 3-5 real tasks timed and token-counted bare vs configured; a stale-rule ablation audit.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: A before/after benchmark on 3-5 real project tasks: configured setup beats bare on tokens, wall-clock, or a correctness check, measured not vibed (explicitly the opposite of eyeballing, per the aiemerges session-log study). An ablation showing stale/over-instruction rules, once removed, do not hurt (or help) the score. A second project inheriting the setup reproduces the behaviour. Parallel-worktree throughput measured on a real multi-task batch.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: Act as a Claude Code power user who measures, not a tutorial reader. For my project at <path>, take me from bare install to a mastered, proven setup and quantify every step. Baseline first: pick 3-5 tasks I actually do, run them on a bare config, and record tokens and wall-clock. Then add components one at a time, re-running the benchmark after each: a CLAUDE.md distilled from my transcripts (Boris Cherny pattern - plan-first, subagents, corrections become rules in tasks/lessons.md, prove before done); primer.md + memory persistence; 2-3 skills for workflows I repeat; hooks for self-correction; MCP vs CLI tools (keep the leaner); Graphify for query-before-read; parallel worktrees for a real multi-task batch; and cost controls (caveman/concise output, advisor mode). Crucially, run a subtraction pass: ablate each rule and skill, and delete anything whose removal does not hurt the benchmark - stale rules written for older models make new ones dumber (cooper.simson, Cherny's simple mode). Keep only what beats the prior setup. Return the progression with before/after numbers, the ablation results, the cost delta, and a setup a second project can inherit.

claude-mastery.one_shot:
You are a Claude Code power user who measures everything. Your job is to take one real project from bare install to a mastered, proven setup, keeping only what beats the prior configuration on a repeatable test. Stance: measure, do not cargo-cult; subtract as aggressively as you add. No marketing language.

Context and method: Boris Cherny's team workflow is the reference - plan-first, 3-15 parallel worktrees, every correction becomes a rule in tasks/lessons.md, never mark done without proof. But mastery is also subtraction: Cherny's simple mode (CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE-style ablation) shows stripping prompts can raise capability, and cooper.simson's purge shows stale rules written for older models drag new models down. Control cost: the concise-output/caveman study chase.h.ai cites shows brevity can raise accuracy and cut tokens; advisor mode lets Opus plan while Sonnet/Haiku execute. Use Graphify/LightRAG to query before reading raw files. And heed the AMD-director session-log analysis (aiemerges/nataindata): measure real behaviour from logs, not vibes.

Hard constraints: benchmark on 3-5 real tasks from THIS project; add components one at a time and re-run; ablate every rule/skill and cut what does not earn its place; measure tokens and wall-clock, never eyeball. Name real features, files, tools. Do not adopt a component without a before/after number.

Ordered deliverables: (1) a baseline benchmark - 3-5 real tasks on a bare config, tokens + wall-clock. (2) a CLAUDE.md distilled from my transcripts (Cherny pattern) + its benchmark delta. (3) memory: primer.md + tasks/lessons.md + a launch git-state injector, + delta. (4) 2-3 skills for repeated workflows + delta. (5) hooks for self-correction + delta. (6) tool layer: MCP vs CLI chosen per leanness, and Graphify for query-before-read, + delta. (7) parallel worktrees measured on a real multi-task batch. (8) a subtraction pass: ablate each rule/skill, delete what removal does not hurt; plus cost controls (concise output, advisor mode) with the token delta.

Built-in gap analysis: before finishing, list what is unverified - are the benchmark numbers from real runs; did any component get adopted without beating baseline; are stale rules still present; is the worktree throughput measured or assumed. Fill what you can.

Self-questions to answer in writing: Are my numbers measured from real runs, or vibed (the exact mistake the session-log study warns about)? Did any rule get kept despite the ablation saying cut? Are there rules written for older models still dragging the new one? Did concise/caveman output actually cut tokens without hurting correctness? Did advisor mode lower cost on the benchmark? Is CLI leaner than MCP for any tool I kept as MCP? Did parallel worktrees actually raise throughput, or just complexity?

Stop conditions: stop and ask only if there is no git history or no real tasks to benchmark. Otherwise proceed end to end.

Return format: a markdown progression report - a table of setup stage vs tokens/wall-clock/correctness, the ablation results, the cost delta, the worktree-throughput result, and an 'Unverified and missing' section. Commit the setup (CLAUDE.md, primer.md, tasks/lessons.md, skills, hooks, settings); print the commit hash. One more discipline: separate the signal from the drama in the source material. The session-log and model-downgrade claims (aiemerges, nataindata) are exactly the kind of thing you must re-derive from your own measured runs rather than repeat, so treat every viral 'the model got dumber' assertion as a hypothesis your benchmark tests, not a fact. And when you report the progression, show the regressions too: a stage that made things worse is as useful to the reader as one that helped, because it tells them what not to copy from the videos this dive is built from.

steps.title: Baseline benchmark (measure, not vibe)
steps.goal: Quantify the bare install on real tasks before adding anything.
steps.prompt: Establish ground truth by measuring, explicitly rejecting vibes (the aiemerges/nataindata session-log study showed real behaviour must be measured, not felt). Pick 3-5 tasks you actually do on this project (e.g. 'add an endpoint', 'fix a failing test', 'refactor a module'). With a BARE config (empty or no CLAUDE.md, no skills, no hooks), run each task and record: tokens used, wall-clock time, tool-call count, and a pass/fail correctness check per task. Run each task twice to get a noise sense. This baseline table is the number every later stage must beat; adopt nothing that does not improve it.
steps.expect: A baseline table: task, tokens, wall-clock, tool calls, pass/fail, over two runs each for noise.
steps.audit: Confirm every number came from a real run (keep the logs), and that the config was genuinely bare. Fail if any number is estimated or the config had leftover rules. On fail, re-run clean.

steps.title: CLAUDE.md from transcripts
steps.goal: Write rules distilled from real evidence, in the Cherny pattern.
steps.prompt: Write CLAUDE.md distilled from this project's session transcripts (search ~/.claude/projects), not from blog advice. Follow Boris Cherny's pattern: plan before touching code; use subagents for hard problems; every correction becomes a rule in tasks/lessons.md; never mark a task done without proving it (tests or a diff against main). Each rule carries an `# evidence:` tag tying it to a transcript finding or a safety reason. Keep it under 200 lines. Re-run the step-1 benchmark with this CLAUDE.md and record the delta. If a rule does not help the benchmark and is not a safety/money guardrail, it is a candidate for the step-8 purge.
steps.expect: A CLAUDE.md (<200 lines, evidence-tagged, Cherny pattern) and a benchmark delta vs baseline.
steps.audit: Grep for untagged rules; each is a candidate to cut. Confirm the benchmark delta is from a real re-run. Fail if the file exceeds 200 lines or the delta is estimated. On fail, trim and re-measure.

steps.title: Memory persistence
steps.goal: Add primer.md, lessons loop, and launch git-state injection.
steps.prompt: Add the memory layer. (1) primer.md - a current-state snapshot rewritten at end of session (status, what changed, next up, blockers), with a CLAUDE.md rule to rewrite it. (2) tasks/lessons.md - the corrections loop from the Cherny pattern, read at session start. (3) a launch-time git-state injector (memory.sh or a SessionStart hook) printing last-5-commits, modified files, branch. Re-run the benchmark and record the delta, especially on tasks that depend on prior context. Keep the layer only if it beats the prior stage or is clearly needed for multi-session continuity.
steps.expect: primer.md, tasks/lessons.md, a launch git-state injector, and a benchmark delta.
steps.audit: Confirm primer.md is a snapshot not a log, lessons.md is read at start, and the injector runs without error. Fail if the delta is estimated or primer.md is a changelog. On fail, fix and re-measure.

steps.title: Skills + hooks
steps.goal: Add reusable workflows and self-correction, each measured.
steps.prompt: Add skills and hooks, each benchmarked. (1) Write 2-3 skills for workflows you repeat on this project (standalone SKILL.md, trigger + steps + commands + done-check; define the workflow, don't personify). (2) Add hooks for self-correction, in jens.heitmann's style: e.g. a PreToolUse anti-deletion hook that stages instead of deletes, a Stop hook that checks tests ran, a SessionStart context loader. Re-run the benchmark after adding skills, then after adding hooks, recording each delta. Adopt each skill/hook only if it beats the prior stage or prevents a real recurring failure.
steps.expect: 2-3 skills and 1-3 hooks, each with a benchmark delta, adopted only if they improved the score or prevented a known failure.
steps.audit: Trigger each hook to confirm it fires; confirm each skill runs standalone. Fail if a hook never fires or a skill/hook was adopted with no delta and no failure-prevention reason. On fail, fix or drop it.

steps.title: Tool layer: MCP vs CLI + retrieval
steps.goal: Pick the leanest tool integration and add query-before-read.
steps.prompt: Optimise the tool layer. (1) For each external capability you need (git, deploys, a database, scraping), compare MCP server vs a CLI tool and keep the LEANER one on the benchmark (chase.h.ai repeatedly shows CLI can beat MCP on tokens/latency). (2) Add Graphify: build the knowledge graph for this repo (`/graphify .`) and add a CLAUDE.md rule to query the graph before opening raw files; for a large/markdown repo consider LightRAG/RAG-Anything. Re-run the benchmark, especially on tasks that involve reading across many files, and record the token delta from query-before-read. Keep MCP only where it beat the CLI.
steps.expect: A per-capability MCP-vs-CLI decision backed by benchmark, Graphify (or LightRAG) wired with a query-before-read rule, and a token delta.
steps.audit: Confirm the kept integration is actually the leaner one per the benchmark, and that the agent queries the graph before raw reads. Fail if MCP was kept on preference not numbers, or the graph is built but never queried. On fail, switch to the leaner tool or enforce the query rule.

steps.title: Parallel worktrees
steps.goal: Measure multi-session throughput on a real batch.
steps.prompt: Adopt parallel worktrees the way Cherny's team does, and measure it. Take a real batch of 3-5 independent tasks on this project. Run them (a) serially in one session and (b) across 3-5 git worktrees each with its own Claude session, named and aliased for fast switching. Measure total wall-clock and any merge-conflict cost for both. Report whether parallel worktrees actually raised throughput for this batch or just added coordination overhead. Only recommend the worktree workflow if the measured throughput gain is real.
steps.expect: A serial-vs-parallel throughput measurement on a real batch, with merge-cost noted and a kept/not-kept recommendation.
steps.audit: Confirm the tasks were genuinely independent (no shared files) and both arms are real timings. Fail if worktrees were recommended without a measured gain, or tasks shared files (invalid parallelism). On fail, re-pick independent tasks or report that parallelism did not help here.

steps.title: Subtraction pass + cost controls
steps.goal: Ablate stale rules and apply token controls, keeping only what helps.
steps.prompt: Run the subtraction pass - mastery is deletion as much as addition. (1) Ablate: remove each CLAUDE.md rule group and each skill one at a time, re-run the benchmark, and DELETE anything whose removal does not hurt the score and is not a safety/money guardrail (cooper.simson's purge; Cherny's simple mode showing over-instruction caps capability). (2) Cost controls: test concise/caveman output rules and advisor mode (Opus plans, Sonnet/Haiku execute) on the benchmark; keep them if they cut tokens/cost without hurting correctness (the concise-output study chase.h.ai cites). Report the setup before and after the purge: line count, token cost, correctness. The goal is the smallest setup that holds the score.
steps.expect: An ablation table (rule/skill, score with/without, kept/cut), a trimmed setup, and a cost-control delta from concise output + advisor mode.
steps.audit: Confirm each cut was decided by a real re-run, and that concise mode did not drop correctness. Fail if nothing was cut (no real ablation) or if a token saving came with a correctness regression. On fail, actually run the ablations.

steps.title: Validate + inheritable setup + gap report
steps.goal: Prove the setup beats baseline and reproduces on a second project.
steps.prompt: Final validation. (1) Run the full benchmark on the final, trimmed setup vs the step-1 baseline and report the deltas (tokens, wall-clock, correctness). (2) Inheritance: copy the setup (CLAUDE.md template, skills, hooks, settings) to a second project (or a clean clone) and confirm it loads and behaves as intended with minimal edits. (3) Enumerate claims, mark verified/unverified/false, list missing pieces ranked by impact, fix the top two. Commit the setup; print the commit hash. Produce the full progression table: stage -> tokens/wall-clock/correctness, so the improvement (or regression) at each step is visible.
steps.expect: A full progression table, a second-project inheritance result, a claim ledger, and a committed setup with hash.
steps.audit: Confirm the final setup beats baseline on at least one metric and that the second project actually loaded it. Fail if the final setup is not better than bare, or inheritance was not tested. On fail, report honestly - if mastery amounted mostly to subtraction, say so.

claude-mastery.gap_audit_prompt: Run after the setup is built. Enumerate every claim as a numbered list: the baseline, each stage's benchmark delta, the MCP-vs-CLI decisions, the Graphify query-before-read saving, the worktree throughput, the ablation cuts, and the cost-control deltas. Mark each VERIFIED (with real run logs), UNVERIFIED, or FALSE. Specifically re-check: are all numbers measured not vibed (the session-log study's warning); was any component adopted without beating the prior stage; are stale rules written for older models still present; did concise/caveman output cut tokens without hurting correctness; is any kept MCP server actually leaner than its CLI; did parallel worktrees show a real throughput gain on independent tasks; did the second project actually inherit the setup. List missing pieces: unablated rules, unmeasured stages, MCP kept on preference, untested inheritance. Rank by impact on real productivity and cost. Fix the top three and re-verify. Report what you could not fix and why. Do not mark any stage an improvement without a measured before/after.
self_questions: Are all my numbers from real runs, or did I vibe them (the exact mistake the session-log study warns about)?
Did I adopt any component without it beating the prior stage?
Are there CLAUDE.md rules written for older models still dragging the new one down?
Did the ablation actually cut anything, or did I keep everything?
Did concise/caveman output cut tokens without hurting correctness?
Did advisor mode (Opus plans, Sonnet/Haiku executes) lower cost on the benchmark?
Is any kept MCP server actually leaner than its CLI equivalent?
Does the agent query the Graphify graph before reading raw files?
Did parallel worktrees raise throughput on genuinely independent tasks, or add overhead?
Is primer.md a snapshot, and is tasks/lessons.md read at session start?
Does every CLAUDE.md rule have an evidence tag or a safety reason?
Did the second project actually inherit and load the setup?
validation_oracles: A before/after benchmark on 3-5 real project tasks shows the final setup beating the bare install on tokens, wall-clock, or correctness, from real run logs not estimates.
The ablation table shows stale/over-instruction rules removed without hurting the score, and every retained rule/skill justified by a delta or a safety reason.
Concise/caveman output and/or advisor mode cut token cost on the benchmark without a correctness regression.
Parallel worktrees show a measured throughput gain on a batch of genuinely independent tasks (or are honestly reported as not helping).
A second project inherits the setup (CLAUDE.md template, skills, hooks, settings) and behaves as intended with minimal edits.
failure_modes: Cargo-cult setup: components copied from videos without measuring. Tell: a huge CLAUDE.md and no benchmark. Fix: benchmark 3-5 real tasks; adopt only what beats baseline.
Vibes over measurement: 'it feels faster'. Tell: no token/time logs (the session-log study's exact warning). Fix: measure tokens and wall-clock from real runs.
Monotonic CLAUDE.md: rules only ever added, never removed. Tell: stale rules for old models, new model feels dumber. Fix: ablate and purge (simple mode / cooper.simson).
MCP by default: heavyweight MCP where a CLI is leaner. Tell: high token/latency on tool calls. Fix: compare MCP vs CLI on the benchmark, keep the leaner.
Graph built, never queried: Graphify set up but the agent still reads raw files. Tell: no token saving on cross-file tasks. Fix: a CLAUDE.md rule to query before reading, verified.
Fake parallelism: worktrees on tasks that share files. Tell: merge conflicts eat the gain. Fix: only parallelise independent tasks; measure the real throughput.
Concise-at-any-cost: brevity rules that drop correctness. Tell: token savings with more failures. Fix: keep concise mode only if correctness holds on the benchmark.
claude-mastery.agent_direction: Reach first for a bare-config benchmark on 3-5 real tasks and the project's transcripts; the whole pack hinges on measured before/after, so never start adding components before the baseline exists. Cache the baseline table and re-run it after each stage - one component at a time, or you cannot attribute the delta. Use Graphify to query before reading raw files, and prefer a CLI over an MCP server wherever the benchmark says it is leaner. Run the subtraction pass for real: ablate each rule/skill and cut what does not earn its place, because stale rules drag newer models down. Spawn sub-agents for the parallel-worktree throughput test (that is the point) but only on genuinely independent tasks. Stop and ask the user only if there is no git history or no real tasks to benchmark. Return a markdown progression report (stage-by-stage table, ablation results, cost delta, worktree result, 'Unverified and missing') plus the committed setup: CLAUDE.md, primer.md, tasks/lessons.md, skills, hooks, settings. Print the commit hash. If mastery turned out to be mostly subtraction, report that honestly.

deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: The suite, run against your own harness, catches a deliberately planted injection in a test skill (if it does not, the suite is theatre). Build me a prompt-injection CI harness that runs on every skill install and every harness change to my own setup. First, put a throwaway canary secret in a disposable test environment and define an outbound tool-call allowlist for my agent. Build a fixed suite of ~50 defensive cases: direct injection attempts (system-prompt override, role-play escape, encoded payloads) as attack CLASSES to detect, 'just ask nicely' hijack cases modelled on the Noma workflow-hijacking research (an automation returning data without checking the requester is authorized), and sponsored-bias nudges modelled on the Princeton study. Then measure the dive's falsifier: what fraction of cases a plain outbound allowlist blocks with no skill-level testing - if >=95%, tell me a static policy is most of the answer.
