steps.title: Compliance and performance gap list
steps.goal: Find liabilities the buyer inherits on closing day.
steps.prompt: For each shortlisted app, check the ten legal traps from the source post: no privacy policy; policy not disclosing data collection; policy not disclosing AI use; policy not naming third-party processors; uploads promised deleted but still stored; public storage buckets; fake testimonials; hard-to-cancel subscriptions; trial auto-charges without reminder; chatbots without self-harm handling. Inspect the live site, the policy text, storage configuration (bucket ACLs), subscription flow, and deletion code paths. The per-user fine figures in the post are claims; replace them with the actual governing rules (GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, state automatic-renewal laws, FTC guidance on reviews and negative-option billing) and mark each for lawyer review. Then measure the five performance gaps on the live app: response compression headers, write batching in code, request waterfall timing, UI update behavior, cache headers. Write compliance_perf_gaps.md with present, absent, unknown, evidence and fix hours.
steps.expect: A 15-row table per deal with evidence links or code references.
steps.audit: Fail if any row is marked absent without evidence. Do not test bucket access by downloading user data; check configuration only.

steps.title: Paper underwriting of three deals
steps.goal: Decide on paper whether the AI rebuild discount is real at this size.
steps.prompt: For each shortlisted deal, build underwriting.csv: asking price, verified trailing-12-month profit (or 'unverified' and excluded), multiple on verified profit, rebuild hours from rebuild_spec.md times the buyer's hourly cost, compliance and performance fix hours, migration cost, and payback months. Run a downside case with revenue down 30% and churn at twice the baseline. Apply the falsifier: rebuild plus migration cost above six months of verified profit, or expected post-migration churn above 10%, fails the deal. Apply caps: price at most 50K USD and at most 3x verified seller's discretionary earnings. Record predictions (hours, churn, payback) in predictions.json with a timestamp so a later actual can be scored against them. Compare to a control: what the same capital earns in a treasury bill over the payback period.
steps.expect: underwriting.csv, predictions.json, and a one-paragraph verdict per deal.
steps.audit: Fail if any input is unverified but used as verified. Recompute payback with a fresh script. Check the downside case is actually computed, not described.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: State which deal, if any, passes, and what remains unproven.
steps.prompt: Assemble final_report.md. For each deal: verified versus claimed revenue difference, tech findings by severity, compliance liabilities, payback base and downside, falsifier result, and a buy, pass or need-more-data verdict for the user to decide on. Write post_close_plan.md for the best deal: day 1 PostHog and credential rotation, weeks 1 to 2 characterization tests, weeks 3 to 10 strangler rebuild of core flows with daily regression tests in CI, monthly churn from the processor against the pre-close cohort. Then a GAPS section listing every source claim (18B USD IPO from 40K USD; public SaaS down roughly half; AI cheapens rebuilds; earned autonomy works unattended; the legal fine figures) as verified, unverified or false with evidence, and every deal number that is still seller-reported. Recommend which professional must review what before any money moves.
steps.expect: final_report.md, post_close_plan.md and a GAPS list.
steps.audit: Fail if a buy verdict rests on any unverified number or if the report omits the lawyer and escrow requirement. Cross-check three numbers against underwriting.csv.

micro-bending-spoons.gap_audit_prompt: You are an independent reviewer of a micro-acquisition package. Open listings.parquet, tech_dd.md files, rebuild_spec.md, compliance_perf_gaps.md, underwriting.csv, predictions.json and final_report.md. List every number and claim that supports a buy or pass verdict. Mark each verified (cite processor export, bank statement, tool output or code line), unverified (name the document that would prove it), or false. Specifically check: revenue reconciled to processor and bank within 5%; multiple computed on verified profit; rebuild hours include migration, support and store review; every core flow has a characterization test; secrets were not pasted into reports; each legal row cites the governing rule rather than a social-media fine figure; the downside case was computed; the falsifier threshold of six months of profit was applied. List missing items such as unrequested documents, unscanned repos, or untested flows. Rank by how much each could change a buy verdict, fix the top three now by recomputing or requesting the missing document in the requests list, and report before and after. End with what cannot be fixed without the seller, a lawyer or an accountant, and confirm no money moves before those reviews.
self_questions: Is the value in the code, or in a search rank, app-store listing or domain that a rebuild could lose?
Did I reconcile revenue to the processor and bank, or to the seller's dashboard?
What share of revenue sits with the top five customers, and what happens if one leaves at handover?
Does the rebuild estimate cover data migration, support load during cutover, and store review delays?
Which legal traps already exist in the seller's app and transfer to me at close?
Which flows does PostHog or the seller's analytics show customers actually use, versus what the code contains?
Is the stack old enough that rebuilding pays, but not so tangled that characterization tests are impossible?
Does the asset purchase agreement transfer IP, domains, accounts and customer contracts cleanly?
Would a treasury bill beat this deal's downside case over the payback period?
Did the earned-autonomy loop check stop_reason, or could refusals have passed as success?
validation_oracles: Read-only processor exports and bank statements reconciled to the listing within 5%.
A lawyer's review of the asset purchase agreement and the compliance gap list; an escrow service holding funds until transfer.
The characterization test suite passing on the old app before the rewrite and on the new app after each strangler step.
Post-close monthly churn from the processor versus the pre-close cohort baseline, with the 10% falsifier threshold.
Actual rebuild hours logged in predictions.json scored against the paper estimate.
failure_modes: Screenshot revenue: seller dashboards overstate. Tell: numbers do not reconcile to deposits. Fix: require processor read-only access and bank statements before shortlisting.

Rank, not code: traffic from one search ranking collapses after migration changes URLs. Tell: Search Console shows most revenue from a few pages. Fix: preserve URLs and redirects; treat SEO as a core flow.
Rewrite before understanding: agents rewrite flows nobody tested. Tell: support tickets spike after cutover. Fix: characterization tests first, strangler migration one flow at a time.
Inherited liability: public buckets or undeleted uploads exist at close. Tell: compliance table rows marked present. Fix: fix before migration and negotiate escrow holdback.
Silent agent failures: refusals returned as HTTP 200 counted as success. Tell: tasks pass but output is empty or a refusal text. Fix: check stop_reason and revoke autonomy below 90% pass rate.
Estimate optimism: hours ignore migration and support. Tell: actual hours exceed the high estimate in month one. Fix: re-underwrite with actuals and stop if payback breaks.
micro-bending-spoons.agent_direction: Start with Acquire.com and Flippa listing data, then stop and hand the shortlist and request lists to the user, because data room access, NDAs and seller contact are the user's actions. Cache listings and every tool output under a deals/ folder per listing. Once repo access exists, spawn one sub-agent per shortlisted repo for step 2 tool runs in isolated worktrees, and review their findings by spot-checking three tool outputs each. Run steps 3 to 5 yourself, since they are judgment-heavy. Never paste secrets found by gitleaks into any report. Never run reverse-engineering tools on apps the user does not own or have written permission to analyze. Stop and ask when revenue cannot be verified, when a legal question decides the verdict, or before any communication with a seller. Return final_report.md as the entry point, with listings.parquet, tech_dd.md files, rebuild_spec.md, compliance_perf_gaps.md, underwriting.csv, predictions.json and post_close_plan.md beside it.

scan-fit-print.mission: Produces a scan-to-parametric-CAD pipeline in which a coding agent takes a mesh of a real object (from the Orbiter smartphone rig, photogrammetry, or a Raspberry Pi LiDAR handheld), fits geometric primitives to the contact surfaces, writes a CadQuery script for a mount with a stated clearance, slices it through a CLI the agent builds itself, and logs iterations-to-fit against the maker's own hand CAD on three objects. Done means three printed parts with caliper-verified fit, a measured scan error budget, and a falsifier verdict on whether agent CAD needs fewer print iterations than hand CAD.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A mechanical design engineer would start with an error budget, not a scan: scanner accuracy, mesh-to-primitive fitting error, printer dimensional error, and the clearance they want, each measured. They would print a clearance test coupon first (holes and pegs at 0.1 to 0.5 mm steps) so the agent's '0.3 mm clearance' means something on this printer and filament. They would fit primitives with RANSAC and report residuals per surface, keep the CAD fully parametric with dimensions named, and verify the scan against calipers on at least three features before trusting it. They would also design for printing: orientation, overhangs, wall thickness, and where to split.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: The Orbiter repo and build docs from Raw Mechatronics; the Peppa Cam build plan (wiring, code and CAD); the LingBot-Map repository from Ant Group's Robbyant team for video-to-3D; the FreeCAD source and docs at github.com/FreeCAD/FreeCAD; CadQuery and build123d docs; PrusaSlicer or OrcaSlicer command-line references; the Y-Pan and Gemma Translator STL and bill-of-materials releases as reference for shipping a device as files. Your own raw data: the photo set or point cloud, caliper readings of the object, and the clearance coupon measurements.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Capture: Orbiter rig or a turntable photo set processed in COLMAP or Meshroom (AliceVision); a printed ArUco or ChArUco board in frame to fix scale. Mesh clean-up: Open3D (statistical outlier removal, Poisson reconstruction), trimesh, or Blender Python. Primitive fitting: pyransac3d or Open3D segment_plane for planes, cylinder fits with least squares, residual RMS per surface. Comparison: CloudCompare cloud-to-mesh distance. CAD: CadQuery or build123d in Python, FreeCAD as fallback, exporting STEP and STL. Slicing: PrusaSlicer --export-gcode or OrcaSlicer CLI wrapped in an agent-built CLI that sets profile, orientation and supports. Prompt pattern from the source set: 'Build yourself a CLI tool to interact with [program]' where no MCP exists.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: The physical test fit on the real object, judged by a go/no-go criterion written before printing. Caliper measurements of printed features versus CAD dimensions. CloudCompare deviation of the scan versus a reference object of known size (a gauge block, a 25 mm calibration cube, or a machined part). The maker's own hand-CAD iteration count on the same objects as the control.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: Act as a mechanical design engineer building a scan-to-fit pipeline. Before any scanning, design and slice a clearance coupon (pegs and holes at 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 mm clearance, 10 mm long) for my printer and filament, and tell me which clearance to adopt from my caliper readings. Then, for each of three objects (a tool handle, a bike mount point, a phone in its case), give a capture protocol for the Orbiter rig or a phone photo set with a ChArUco board for scale, processed in COLMAP or Meshroom. Write a Python script with Open3D and pyransac3d that cleans the mesh, fits planes and cylinders to the contact surfaces I mark, and reports residual RMS per surface. Validate the scan against three caliper measurements per object and stop if error exceeds 0.3 mm. Write a CadQuery script per object that builds a mount referencing the fitted primitives, with named parameters for clearance, wall thickness and fastener holes, exporting STEP and STL. Build yourself a CLI tool around PrusaSlicer that takes STL, orientation and profile and returns G-code plus estimated time and material. After each print I will give you caliper readings and a fit verdict; update parameters and log iterations-to-fit. In parallel I will hand-CAD the same three parts. Report iterations per object for both methods and say whether agent CAD lost on all three.

scan-fit-print.one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are a mechanical design engineer and automation developer. Goal: prove or disprove that an agent can turn a scan of a real object into a parametric part that fits on the first or second print. Source claims to test: Orbiter promises 'a perfect fit on the first try' from a smartphone scan; Peppa Cam says a Pi LiDAR handheld is fine 'for most scanning jobs'; a Claude-to-Blender demo built a whole scene as Python; the 'build yourself a CLI tool' pattern lets an agent control any program without an MCP; text-to-CAD sites claim complete CAD models from a sentence.

CONTEXT
- Scanners: Orbiter (smartphone rig), photogrammetry via COLMAP or Meshroom, Peppa Cam Raspberry Pi LiDAR, LingBot-Map video-to-3D.
- Geometry: Open3D, trimesh, pyransac3d, CloudCompare.
- CAD: CadQuery or build123d (Python), FreeCAD fallback, Blender Python only for visualization.
- Slicing: PrusaSlicer or OrcaSlicer CLI.
- Hardware: the user's FDM printer, calipers, a ChArUco board printed at known scale.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
1. Every dimension in the CAD is a named parameter traceable to a fitted primitive or a caliper reading.
2. The scan is not trusted until three caliper checks per object agree within 0.3 mm.
3. Clearance is chosen from a printed coupon on this printer and filament, not assumed.
4. Write the go/no-go fit criterion per object before printing it.
5. The hand-CAD control is done by the user without seeing the agent's CAD.

DELIVERABLES IN ORDER
1. coupon.py (CadQuery), coupon.stl and the recommended clearance after the user's measurements.
2. capture_protocol.md for each object and scanner.
3. fit_primitives.py: clean mesh, segment marked contact regions, fit planes and cylinders, report residual RMS and the fitted parameters as JSON.
4. scan_check.md: caliper vs scan for three features per object; CloudCompare deviation vs a reference object.
5. One CadQuery script per object with STEP and STL output and a parameter table.
6. slicecli: an agent-built command-line wrapper around PrusaSlicer with orientation, profile and support flags, returning G-code path, time and grams.
7. fit_log.csv: object, method (agent or hand), iteration, parameters changed, caliper readings, fit verdict.
8. report.md with iterations-to-fit per object and method and the falsifier verdict.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
Before finishing, list in GAPS: surfaces where primitive fitting failed (organic shapes like a tool handle grip); scale uncertainty; printer drift between iterations; any object where the hand CAD and agent CAD used different clearances; claims you could not test (for example LingBot-Map accuracy if not run). Fill gaps you can, such as re-fitting with a different primitive or adding a freeform offset surface from the mesh, and record the result.

SELF-QUESTIONS
- Which surfaces actually bear the load or locate the part, and did I fit only those?
- Is the scan scaled from a known reference, or is photogrammetry scale arbitrary?
- Is my clearance compensating for printer error that a slicer setting (horizontal expansion, elephant-foot compensation) should fix instead?
- Does print orientation change the fit dimension more than my clearance?
- For organic shapes, should the part be a mesh offset instead of primitives?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop and report if scan error exceeds 0.3 mm after two capture attempts, or if after three iterations an object still fails fit; record which error source dominated.

RETURN FORMAT
A table of iterations-to-fit by object and method, falsifier verdict, file list, GAPS, and self-question answers.

steps.title: Ground truth: printer coupon and scanner accuracy
steps.goal: Measure what this printer and scanner can actually hold before designing anything.
steps.prompt: Write coupon.py in CadQuery: a plate with pegs and matching holes at 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 and 0.5 mm diametral clearance, 10 mm diameter and 10 mm deep, labeled by embossed numbers, plus a 25 mm calibration cube. Export STL and give PrusaSlicer settings to print it in the same orientation and material planned for the parts. Ask the user for caliper readings of every peg, hole and cube face, and for which pegs slide, press, or do not fit. From those readings compute the printer's dimensional bias and choose the slip-fit and press-fit clearances. Then have the user scan the calibration cube and one machined reference (or a gauge block) with each scanner they have, Orbiter rig or phone photogrammetry with a ChArUco board in frame, and compute scan scale error and CloudCompare deviation against nominal.
steps.expect: coupon.stl, a clearance recommendation with measured bias, and a scanner accuracy table in mm.
steps.audit: Fail if clearance is recommended without user caliper data or if scan scale is not anchored to a known reference. If scan error exceeds 0.3 mm, change capture settings before step 2.

steps.title: Capture and clean three object scans
steps.goal: Produce clean, scaled meshes of a tool handle, a bike mount point and a phone in its case.
steps.prompt: Write capture_protocol.md for each object: lighting, matte spray or chalk on shiny surfaces, ChArUco board placement, number and spacing of photos (for photogrammetry 60 to 120 images with 70% overlap), turntable or Orbiter settings, and for the bike mount a handheld protocol since it cannot move. After the user captures, process in COLMAP or Meshroom, then write clean_mesh.py with Open3D: statistical outlier removal, Poisson reconstruction or keep the original mesh, hole filling, scale from the board, and alignment so the main contact plane lies on XY. Export each as PLY and STL with a metadata JSON listing source images, scale factor and vertex count. Ask the user for three caliper measurements per object on features visible in the scan. If a Peppa Cam LiDAR scan exists, process it too.
steps.expect: Three clean meshes, metadata files, and a table comparing three caliper readings per object to scan measurements.
steps.audit: Fail any object whose caliper-to-scan difference exceeds 0.3 mm on any check; recapture with more images or matte spray. Note the error in the GAPS list.

steps.title: Fit primitives to contact surfaces
steps.goal: Turn noisy mesh regions into exact planes, cylinders and offsets the CAD can reference.
steps.prompt: Write fit_primitives.py. Inputs: a cleaned mesh and a JSON of contact regions the user marks (vertex indices selected in Blender or MeshLab, or bounding boxes). For each region, fit a plane with Open3D segment_plane, a cylinder with pyransac3d or least squares, or a sphere, choosing by lowest residual RMS. Output primitives.json: type, parameters (normal and offset, axis and radius), residual RMS, inlier fraction. For regions with RMS above 0.2 mm (likely organic, like a grip), output an offset surface instead: the mesh region offset outward by the chosen clearance, exported as a separate STL the CAD can subtract. Render a quick check image in Blender headless showing primitives overlaid on the mesh. Print a summary table of every region with type, RMS and inlier fraction so the user can veto a fit before CAD.
steps.expect: primitives.json per object, optional offset STLs for organic regions, and an overlay image.
steps.audit: Fail if any primitive has inlier fraction under 0.8. Check fitted cylinder radii against caliper diameters within 0.15 mm; if not, refit with tighter region selection.

steps.title: Parametric CAD and an agent-built slicer CLI
steps.goal: Generate printable, parametric mounts and slice them from the command line.
steps.prompt: For each object write a CadQuery script that loads primitives.json and builds the part around the fitted surfaces: contact faces offset by the chosen clearance, wall thickness 2.4 mm minimum, fillets on stress corners, fastener holes or strap slots, and boolean subtraction of any offset STL. All dimensions are named parameters at the top of the file with comments citing their source (primitive ID, caliper reading, coupon). Export STEP and STL. Then build yourself a CLI tool, slicecli, around PrusaSlicer: arguments for STL path, printer profile, filament, orientation (rotation in degrees), supports on or off, and output path; it returns G-code path, estimated time and grams, and fails loudly on slicer errors. Write the go/no-go fit criterion for each part before slicing.
steps.expect: Three CadQuery scripts, STEP and STL files, slicecli with help text, sliced G-code, and written fit criteria.
steps.audit: Re-import each STL in trimesh and check it is watertight and the clearance gap measured between part and mesh equals the parameter within 0.05 mm. Fail any part needing supports inside the contact surfaces.

steps.title: Print, measure, iterate, and run the hand-CAD control
steps.goal: Log iterations-to-fit for agent CAD versus hand CAD on the same objects.
steps.prompt: After each print, ask the user for caliper readings on every named contact dimension and a fit verdict against the written criterion. Compute the error per parameter and update only the parameters with measured error, logging iteration, changed parameter, old and new value, and reason in fit_log.csv. Maximum three iterations per object. In parallel the user designs the same three parts by hand in their usual CAD tool, without seeing the agent's files, and logs their own iterations in the same CSV with method set to hand. If an object fails three times, classify the dominant error source: scan, fitting, CAD logic, or printer. For comparison, also generate one of the parts from a text-to-CAD website prompt and log whether it fits at all.
steps.expect: fit_log.csv with every iteration for both methods and a short error-source note per failed object.
steps.audit: Fail if any parameter change is not justified by a measurement. Check the hand control used the same printer, filament and clearance coupon.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Deliver the falsifier verdict and list what is unproven.
steps.prompt: Write report.md: per object, iterations-to-fit for agent and hand methods, final caliper error per contact dimension, scan accuracy, primitive residuals, and print time and material. State the falsifier: if agent CAD needed more iterations than hand CAD on all three objects, the scan-to-parametric step is not ready and the fitting step, not the scanner, is the bottleneck; say which error source dominated. Then a GAPS section: each source claim (perfect fit first try, Pi LiDAR good for most jobs, LLMs write Blender and CAD scripts, build-your-own CLI, text-to-CAD) marked verified, unverified or false with the fit_log row or measurement that decides it; objects or scanners not tested; and anything from LingBot-Map not run. Package the three parts as a release folder with STEP, STL, parameter table and bill of materials, the way Y-Pan and Gemma Translator ship.
steps.expect: report.md, GAPS list, and a release folder per part.
steps.audit: Recompute iteration counts from fit_log.csv with a fresh script. Fail if any claim is marked verified without a cited measurement.

scan-fit-print.gap_audit_prompt: You are an independent reviewer of a scan-to-fit pipeline. Open the coupon results, capture protocols, meshes and metadata, primitives.json files, CadQuery scripts, slicecli, fit_log.csv and report.md. List every claim in report.md. For each, mark verified (cite the measurement, file or log row), unverified (say what measurement would prove it), or false. Check specifically: scale was anchored to a known reference; caliper-to-scan checks exist for every object; clearance came from the coupon on the same printer and filament; every CAD parameter cites a source; parameter changes between iterations cite a measurement; the hand-CAD control used the same constraints and was done blind; the falsifier comparison used the same fit criterion for both methods. List missing pieces such as untested scanners or organic regions forced into primitives. Rank problems by whether they could reverse the agent-versus-hand verdict, fix the top three now (for example by refitting a region or recomputing iteration counts), and report before and after. End with what needs another print or scan to resolve.
self_questions: Which surfaces locate or load each part, and did I fit only those rather than the whole mesh?
Is photogrammetry scale anchored to the ChArUco board or calibration cube, and by how much could it be off?
Is the measured printer bias handled by slicer compensation or baked into clearance, and is that consistent across iterations?
Did print orientation put a critical diameter on the Z axis where layer steps distort it?
For the tool handle grip, would a mesh offset fit better than any primitive?
Does the bike mount scan, taken handheld on a fixed object, have more error than the turntable scans?
Did the hand-CAD control get the same coupon data and fit criterion?
Did slicecli fail loudly on a bad profile, or could it silently use defaults?
Which single error source would I fix first if all three objects failed?
validation_oracles: The physical fit on each real object, judged against a go/no-go criterion written before printing.
Caliper measurements of printed contact features versus CadQuery parameters, within the coupon-derived tolerance.
CloudCompare deviation of scans versus a calibration cube or gauge block of known size.
The user's blind hand-CAD iteration counts on the same three objects, as the control.
PrusaSlicer slicing each STL without errors and trimesh confirming each part is watertight.
failure_modes: Unscaled scan: photogrammetry mesh is uniformly 2% off. Tell: every printed dimension misses by the same ratio. Fix: scale from the ChArUco board or a reference cube in frame.
Fitting the wrong surface: agent fits a cosmetic face instead of the locating one. Tell: part sits but rocks or slides. Fix: user marks contact regions explicitly; fit only those.

Clearance fighting printer bias: holes print undersized and clearance is raised every iteration. Tell: iterations change the same parameter in the same direction. Fix: apply slicer XY hole compensation from the coupon, reset clearance.
Organic shapes forced into primitives: grip fit fails with high residual. Tell: RMS above 0.2 mm on that region. Fix: mesh offset subtraction for organic regions.
Orientation distortion: critical bore printed vertically becomes oval. Tell: caliper shows different diameters across axes. Fix: reorient in slicecli or split the part.
Silent slicer defaults: CLI ignores a misspelled profile name. Tell: print time differs from expected. Fix: slicecli validates profile names and exits non-zero.
scan-fit-print.agent_direction: Begin with the clearance coupon; it is cheap and makes every later number meaningful. Use Python throughout (CadQuery, Open3D, trimesh, pyransac3d) and call Blender headless only for overlay renders. Cache every mesh, primitives.json and STL with a version suffix per iteration so fits can be compared. Spawn a sub-agent to build slicecli in parallel with step 3, and review it by passing a bad profile name and confirming it fails. Physical steps (printing, scanning, caliper readings, hand CAD) belong to the user: write precise instructions, then pause and wait for measurements rather than inventing them. Never fabricate caliper data or fit verdicts. Stop and ask when a scan fails accuracy twice or when the user's printer or filament changes mid-study. Return report.md as the entry point with coupon files, capture protocols, meshes, primitives.json, CadQuery scripts, slicecli, fit_log.csv and a release folder per part.

benchmark-your-brain.mission: Produces a six-week self-experiment that runs the SkillOpt-style benchmark-gated loop on a human learner: the last 60 days of saves (a DejaViewed parquet export qualifies) become the study set, held-out retrieval quizzes become the eval set, and a coach skill rewrites the study playbook only when the next held-out score beats the last. A plain-flashcard control topic runs alongside. Done means per-topic learning curves, a delayed retention test, and a falsifier verdict on whether the coach loop beats flashcards, plus a list of topics that never stick.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A learning scientist would design this as a within-subject experiment: topics matched for difficulty and randomly assigned to coach and control conditions, questions written and frozen before study begins, and a delayed test one to two weeks after the last session, because immediate scores mostly measure short-term memory. They would grade with a rubric written in advance, ideally scored blind by a second model or person, and compute the minimum effect detectable with 15 questions per topic. They would use established mechanisms as baselines, retrieval practice and spacing, not invent new ones, and they would watch for question leakage: if the generator sees the study notes, held-out items stop being held out.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: The user's own saves export (DejaViewed parquet with titles, captions, transcripts and takeaways), the user's exported Claude or ChatGPT history (conversations.json) for re-asked questions, the Microsoft SkillOpt repository (github.com/microsoft/SkillOpt) for the accept-only-if-it-beats-the-eval rule, Karpathy's autoresearch loop and the bilevel outer-loop write-up, the FSRS scheduler (open-spaced-repetition) and Anki for the control condition, and the primary studies: Roediger and Karpicke 2006 on the testing effect and Cepeda et al. 2006 on distributed practice. O*NET task lists and the Anthropic Economic Index if topics are chosen for job relevance.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Python and pandas or DuckDB on the parquet; embedding clustering (sentence-transformers plus HDBSCAN or k-means with k=3 to 4) to form topics; Claude to generate questions from source transcripts with a separate context that never sees the study notes; a frozen item bank with item IDs; a rubric-graded short-answer format scored 0 to 2; FSRS via py-fsrs or Anki for the control topic; a coach skill implementing SkillOpt's rule (propose playbook edit, accept only if next held-out score beats the incumbent); an issues table where each study session logs what failed, rewritten in batch weekly, as in the self-improving skills post. Analysis: paired comparison of coach versus control with bootstrap intervals; learning curves per topic; delayed-test retention ratio.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: A delayed test 14 days after the last session, graded blind by a second grader who does not know the condition. Where possible an external task: a SQL topic checked by solving Database Detective or SQLBolt exercises; a coding topic checked by a build that runs. The control topic studied with FSRS flashcards for the same minutes. A frozen item bank with a hash recorded before week 1.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: Act as a learning scientist running a six-week within-subject experiment on me. Load my saves export (DejaViewed parquet) from the last 60 days. Cluster saves into topics with embeddings and pick four topics of similar size and difficulty; randomly assign three to the coach condition and one to a plain-flashcard control, and record the assignment and seed. For each topic, generate 15 held-out retrieval questions plus a 2-point rubric per question in a separate context that sees only the source transcripts, never my study notes; freeze the bank and record its SHA-256. Write the study playbook v1 (spacing, explain-back, build-a-thing, game) and a coach skill that proposes one playbook change per week and accepts it only if my next held-out score on coach topics beats the incumbent, SkillOpt style. The control topic uses FSRS flashcards for the same minutes per week. Each study session logs issues to a table; the coach reads them. Monthly, mine my exported chat history for questions I re-asked and add them as forced items to a separate bank. At week 6 plus 14 days, give a delayed test graded blind by a second grader. Report learning curves per topic, coach minus control with bootstrap intervals, the minimum detectable effect, topics that never stuck, and whether the falsifier fired.

benchmark-your-brain.one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are a learning scientist and agent engineer. You will run the benchmark-gated skill-optimization loop on a person instead of a prompt. Source claims to test: SkillOpt rejects any skill edit that does not beat the benchmark and beats hand-written prompts; a bilevel outer 'coach' loop is about 5x better on Karpathy's autoresearch benchmark; skills that log their own failures and get batch-rewritten improve; turning saves into quizzes beats passive watching; mining chat history yields better instructions. Treat each as a hypothesis.

CONTEXT
- Study set: the user's saves from the last 60 days; DejaViewed parquet has titles, captions, transcripts, takeaways.
- Eval set: held-out retrieval questions generated from source transcripts.
- Control: FSRS spaced-repetition flashcards (py-fsrs or Anki).
- Optional input: exported Claude or ChatGPT history (conversations.json).
- Budget: about 20 minutes per topic per week of honest self-quizzing.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
1. Item bank frozen before week 1; record its SHA-256. No question is edited after the user sees it.
2. Questions are generated in a context that sees only source material, never study notes, playbooks or prior answers.
3. The coach changes at most one playbook element per week and the change is kept only if the next held-out score on coach topics beats the incumbent.
4. The control topic gets equal minutes and no coach.
5. Quizzes are taken cold: no notes, no search, no AI. Scores are self-reported; the agent must not invent them.
6. Chat-history mining stays local; redact names, emails and credentials before any analysis.

DELIVERABLES IN ORDER
1. topics.json: clusters, chosen topics, difficulty proxy, random assignment with seed.
2. item_bank.parquet: 15 held-out items per topic with rubric, weekly sampling plan, hash.
3. playbook_v1.md and coach skill (prompt plus rules) with the accept-only-if-better gate.
4. session_log.parquet and issues.parquet schemas, plus the weekly script that samples 5 items per topic, collects scores, and runs the coach.
5. chat_mining.py: local pass that finds questions the user asked more than once.
6. analysis.md at week 6 plus 14 days: learning curves, coach minus control with bootstrap intervals, minimum detectable effect, blind delayed-test results, never-stuck topics, falsifier verdict.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
Write GAPS: weeks with missed quizzes; any item that leaked into study material; topics whose difficulty was mismatched; items the second grader scored differently by more than one point; claims you could not test. Fill gaps you can, for example replacing a leaked item from the reserve bank and marking the swap.

SELF-QUESTIONS
- Are the coach and control topics comparable in difficulty and prior knowledge, and how do I know?
- With 15 items and 5 sampled per week, what is the smallest improvement I could detect?
- Could held-out items have leaked through study notes the generator produced?
- Is a week-over-week rise just practice on repeated items rather than learning?
- Did the coach's accepted edits improve the delayed test, or only the next-week quiz?

STOP CONDITIONS
Pause and ask if the user misses two consecutive weeks, if fewer than three topics have enough saves for 15 items, or if the second grader disagrees with self-grading on more than 30% of items.

RETURN FORMAT
Falsifier verdict, learning curve table per topic, coach minus control with interval, never-stuck topics, the file list, GAPS, and self-question answers.

steps.title: Ground truth: saves, topics and assignment
steps.goal: Form comparable topics from the raw saves and assign conditions randomly.
steps.prompt: Load the saves export (DejaViewed parquet or equivalent) and filter to the last 60 days. For each save, build text from title, caption, transcript and takeaways; drop items with under 50 words of usable text and report how many. Embed with sentence-transformers (all-MiniLM-L6-v2 is enough), cluster with HDBSCAN or k-means, and name clusters from their top terms. Pick four clusters with at least 8 saves each and similar text volume. Ask the user to rate prior knowledge 1 to 5 per topic and use it as a difficulty proxy. Randomly assign three topics to coach and one to control with a recorded seed; if prior-knowledge ratings differ by more than 1 point between control and the coach mean, redraw and log it. Write topics.json with members, volume, prior rating, condition and seed.
steps.expect: topics.json with four topics, member save IDs, prior ratings, assignments and seed, plus a count of dropped saves.
steps.audit: Fail if the control topic is chosen by preference instead of the seed, or if any topic lacks enough source text for 15 distinct questions. Spot-read 3 saves per topic to confirm the cluster is coherent.

steps.title: Freeze the held-out item bank
steps.goal: Create an eval set the study process can never see.
steps.prompt: In a fresh context that receives only source transcripts and captions for one topic at a time, generate 20 retrieval questions per topic: mix of recall, explain-why, and apply-to-new-case, each with a model answer and a 0 to 2 rubric (2 complete and correct, 1 partial, 0 wrong or blank). Keep 15 as the bank and 5 as a reserve for replacing leaked items. Check each question is answerable from the sources, not trivia about the creator. Write item_bank.parquet with item ID, topic, type, question, rubric, model answer, and reserve flag, then compute its SHA-256 and store it in bank_hash.txt. Write a weekly sampling plan: 5 items per topic per week, balanced so each item appears at most twice across six weeks, plus the full 15 on the delayed test.
steps.expect: item_bank.parquet with 80 items, bank_hash.txt and sampling_plan.csv.
steps.audit: Have a second model answer every question from the sources alone; fail any item it cannot answer or answers ambiguously, and replace from reserve. Confirm the generation context had no access to notes or playbooks.

steps.title: Playbook v1, coach skill and logging
steps.goal: Implement the benchmark-gated coach and the self-logging study sessions.
steps.prompt: Write playbook_v1.md for coach topics: spacing schedule (sessions on days 1, 3 and 7 of each week), one active format per session chosen from explain-back aloud, build-a-thing, teach-a-friend summary or a game, and a 20-minute cap. Write the coach skill: it reads last week's quiz scores per item and topic, issues.parquet entries, and the playbook; it proposes exactly one change with a stated hypothesis; the change becomes the candidate playbook; after the next quiz, the candidate is kept only if mean held-out score on coach topics beats the incumbent's, otherwise reverted, mirroring SkillOpt's reject rule. Write the session logger: after each session the user records minutes, format used and one line on what failed; these go to issues.parquet. Write the control routine: FSRS flashcards built from the same source material, same minutes.
steps.expect: playbook_v1.md, coach_skill.md, logger script, control card deck, and table schemas.
steps.audit: Simulate two weeks with made-up scores clearly marked SIMULATED and confirm the coach reverts a change that lowered scores. Delete simulated rows afterward. Fail if the coach can edit more than one element or read the item bank.

steps.title: Weekly loop and chat-history mining
steps.goal: Run six weeks of quizzes and coach updates, adding re-asked questions monthly.
steps.prompt: Each week: present the planned 5 items per topic cold, one at a time; the user answers without notes; grade with the rubric and show the model answer after the user commits; record scores in session_log.parquet. Then run the coach. Never fill in a score the user did not give. Monthly, run chat_mining.py on the user's exported conversations.json locally: redact names, emails, phone numbers and keys; find user questions that are semantically near-duplicates across different dates (embedding cosine above 0.85); map them to topics; write them to a separate forced_items bank, not the held-out bank, so they do not contaminate the eval. Print a weekly dashboard: score per topic per week, accepted and rejected coach changes, minutes studied. Flag any week a topic score drops by more than two items.
steps.expect: Six weeks of session_log rows, a coach decision log, forced_items.parquet, and weekly dashboards.
steps.audit: Fail any week where a topic's minutes differ from the control by more than 25%, or where an item was asked more often than the sampling plan allows. Verify the bank hash weekly.

steps.title: Delayed test with blind grading
steps.goal: Measure retention, not short-term recall.
steps.prompt: Fourteen days after the last study session, give the full 15-item bank for every topic in random order, cold. Collect the user's written answers. Grade twice: the user self-grades with the rubric, and a second grader (a separate model context or a person) grades the same answers without being told the condition of each topic. Compute agreement and use the second grader's scores where they differ. Where a topic has an external task, run it: for a SQL topic, time to solve three Database Detective or SQLBolt exercises; for a coding topic, whether a small build from memory runs. Write delayed.parquet and grader agreement statistics. Also give the 5 forced items from chat-history mining as a separate, unscored-for-the-verdict section, so their retention is visible without contaminating the comparison.
steps.expect: delayed.parquet with two grades per answer, an agreement rate, and external task results.
steps.audit: Fail if the second grader saw condition labels or the playbook. If agreement is under 70%, sharpen the rubric wording and regrade only with the second grader, noting it.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Decide whether the coach loop beats flashcards and list what remains unproven.
steps.prompt: Write analysis.md. Show learning curves per topic across six weeks. Compute coach minus control on the delayed test using second-grader scores, with a bootstrap 95% interval over items, and state the minimum detectable effect given the item count. Report the retention ratio (delayed score divided by week-6 score) per topic. List never-stuck topics: delayed score below 50% of maximum. Answer the falsifier: are delayed held-out scores on coach topics no better than the flashcard control? Then a GAPS section: each source claim (SkillOpt's benchmark gate beats hand prompts; the bilevel loop is about 5x better; self-logging skills improve; quizzes beat passive review; chat mining personalizes) marked verified, unverified or false for this one-person experiment, plus missed weeks, leaked items, and limits of a single subject.
steps.expect: analysis.md with curves, interval, retention ratios, never-stuck list, falsifier verdict and GAPS.
steps.audit: Recompute the coach minus control interval from delayed.parquet with a fresh script. Fail if conclusions generalize beyond one person or if immediate quiz gains are presented as retention.

benchmark-your-brain.gap_audit_prompt: You are an independent reviewer of a six-week benchmark-your-brain experiment. Open topics.json, item_bank.parquet, bank_hash.txt, sampling_plan.csv, session_log.parquet, issues.parquet, the coach decision log, delayed.parquet and analysis.md. List every claim in analysis.md and mark each verified (cite the table and computation), unverified (state what data would settle it), or false. Check: the bank hash never changed; no held-out item appears in study notes, playbooks or forced items; the control topic was assigned by the recorded seed and got comparable minutes; each coach change was accepted only after beating the incumbent score; delayed grading used a grader blind to condition; no score was entered by the agent without user input; conclusions are limited to one subject and the stated minimum detectable effect. List missing pieces: missed weeks, topics with too few items, external tasks not run. Rank problems by whether they could reverse the falsifier verdict, fix the top three now (for example regrading with the blind grader or recomputing intervals), and report before and after. End with what only another cohort, a longer delay, or a second learner could answer.
self_questions: Are coach and control topics matched in difficulty and prior knowledge, or did I pick an easy control?
Could any held-out question have appeared in study notes or a generated summary?
With 15 items per topic, is the effect I hope for even detectable?
Is the weekly score rising because items repeat, not because knowledge grows?
Did the coach ever accept a change on a noise-level difference of one item?
Are my self-grades systematically kinder than the blind grader's?
Which saves were too thin to support real questions, and did they bias topic choice?
Did chat-history mining surface re-asked questions I actually need, and were they kept out of the eval bank?
Is the Glenn Gould idea of learning away from the instrument (explain-back without notes) tested by any playbook change?
What would I drop: which topic never stuck and should be re-approached or abandoned?
validation_oracles: A delayed test 14 days after the last session, graded by a second grader blind to condition.
The flashcard control topic on FSRS with matched minutes, as the comparison arm.
bank_hash.txt matching the item bank at every weekly check, proving the eval was frozen.
External tasks where available: Database Detective or SQLBolt exercises for SQL topics, a working build for coding topics.
An independent recomputation of the coach-minus-control interval from delayed.parquet.
failure_modes: Eval leakage: question generator saw the study notes, so quizzes test memorized notes. Tell: near-perfect scores in week 1. Fix: regenerate from sources only and replace leaked items from reserve.
Noise-chasing coach: accepts edits on one-item differences. Tell: playbook flips back and forth weekly. Fix: require a margin at least the week-to-week standard deviation before accepting.
Unmatched control: the control topic is easier or already known. Tell: control prior-knowledge rating differs by 2 or more. Fix: redraw with seed before week 1.
Repetition masquerading as learning: same items each week. Tell: scores rise on repeated items only. Fix: follow the sampling plan and analyze first-exposure items separately.
Self-grading drift: rubric applied more kindly over time. Tell: blind grader disagreement rises across weeks. Fix: use blind grades for all conclusions.
Dropout: missed weeks break the loop. Tell: gaps in session_log. Fix: schedule quizzes as a recurring routine and pause the coach on missed weeks.
benchmark-your-brain.agent_direction: Start from the local saves export with pandas or DuckDB; no network needed except embedding model download. Cache embeddings, topics.json and the frozen bank; never regenerate the bank after week 1. Use a separate sub-agent context for question generation and another for blind grading, and never give either the playbook or condition labels. Run the weekly loop as a scheduled routine that prompts the user and waits; do not proceed without real answers and never invent scores. Keep chat-history mining strictly local with redaction before any model call. Stop and ask when the user misses two weeks, when topics lack material, or when grader agreement is under 70%. Return analysis.md as the entry point with topics.json, item_bank.parquet, bank_hash.txt, sampling_plan.csv, playbook versions, coach decision log, session_log.parquet, issues.parquet, forced_items.parquet and delayed.parquet.

offline-ai-appliances.mission: Produces a working single-purpose offline AI appliance in two stages: first an exact rebuild of Google's Gemma Translator on a Raspberry Pi 5 to learn its deployment script, model stack and thermal limits, then a fork into a 'paperwork reader' that photographs a letter, runs local OCR, summarizes it, flags bills and deadlines, and reads it aloud with Pocket TTS, in a printed case. Done means measured per-page latency and accuracy on 20 real letters, a packet capture proving zero network egress, and a two-week trial log from one non-technical person, judged against the falsifier: more than about 10 s per page or reverting to a phone app within a week.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: An embedded product engineer would set a latency and accuracy budget per stage (capture, OCR, summarize, TTS) and measure each on the target board under sustained thermal load, not one cold run. They would prove offline by test, not by design intent: firewall egress, capture packets, and run the full flow with radios disabled. They would build a labeled test set of real letters, measure character error rate and bill-flag precision and recall, and design for the failure that matters most to an elderly user, a missed due date, by making the box say what it is unsure about. They would also run a short usability protocol with the actual person, observing first use without helping.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: The Gemma Translator repository with its deployment script, parts list (battery, touchscreen, speaker, micro keyboard) and STL files; model cards and weights for Moonshine (speech recognition, Useful Sensors), Gemma (Google), Kyutai Pocket TTS (100M parameters, voice cloning), and Baidu Unlimited OCR (3B, MIT license); llama.cpp and its GGUF quantization docs; Raspberry Pi 5 thermal and power documentation (vcgencmd, 5V 5A supply); Jetson Orin Nano docs if used; Sharp Memory Display datasheet for a low-power status screen; and 20 real letters from the intended user's mail, with consent, as the test set.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: Raspberry Pi OS 64-bit, Python, llama.cpp or the repo's runtime, GGUF quantization at Q4_K_M and Q8_0 for comparison, Unsloth or Soup only if a small summarizer needs fine-tuning on letter types. Measurement: time.perf_counter per stage, p50 and p95 over 20 pages, vcgencmd measure_temp and get_throttled during a 30-minute soak, a USB power meter for watts. Accuracy: jiwer character error rate against hand-transcribed letters; precision and recall for bill and deadline flags against hand labels. Offline proof: nftables output drop rule, tcpdump on all interfaces during the full flow, ss -tupn for open sockets. Case: CadQuery or the repo's STL modified for camera mount and speaker. Trial: on-device local log of button presses and pages read.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: A tcpdump capture showing zero outbound packets during 20 pages processed. Hand-transcribed ground truth for 20 letters scored by jiwer. Bill and deadline labels made by a second person before the box sees the letters. The trial user's own usage log and a short interview after two weeks. The upstream Gemma Translator reaching its published roughly 7 tokens per second on your build, as the baseline that your setup is sound.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: Act as an embedded AI product engineer. Stage 1: clone the Gemma Translator repo and build it exactly as published on a Raspberry Pi 5 with active cooling and a 5V 5A supply. Measure tokens per second against the published roughly 7, per-stage latency for Moonshine, Gemma and TTS, and temperature and throttling over a 30-minute soak; document every deviation from the repo. Stage 2: fork it into a paperwork reader: camera capture, Baidu Unlimited OCR (or a smaller fallback if it will not fit or run fast enough), a quantized Gemma summarizer with a fixed output template (sender, what it is, amount, due date, action needed, confidence), and Kyutai Pocket TTS reading the summary aloud. Build a 20-letter test set with consent, hand-transcribed and hand-labeled for bills and deadlines by a second person. Report p50 and p95 seconds per page, character error rate, and bill-flag precision and recall. Prove offline: nftables drop on output, tcpdump during all 20 pages, zero packets. Design a printed case with camera mount and a big button. Then a two-week trial with one non-technical person: local usage log, no remote telemetry, interview at the end. Apply the falsifier: over about 10 s per page or reverting to a phone app within a week means the form factor is not earning its keep.

offline-ai-appliances.one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are an embedded AI product engineer building a one-job offline appliance for a non-technical person. Source claims to test: Gemma Translator runs speech recognition (Moonshine), translation (Gemma) and TTS on a Raspberry Pi 5 with no network at about 7 tokens per second, 'enough to hold a conversation', and is a weekend build from its BOM and STLs; Baidu Unlimited OCR (3B, MIT) reads 100-page PDFs in one pass with tables and reading order intact; Kyutai Pocket TTS clones voices locally at 6x real time; Qwen 3.8 27B fits a 24GB card; Soup fine-tunes on a 4GB GPU. Vendor benchmarks are claims until measured on your board.

CONTEXT
- Base: Gemma Translator repo, deployment script, BOM, STL case.
- Parts bin: Unlimited OCR, Pocket TTS, Moonshine, quantized Gemma via llama.cpp; Jetson Orin Nano as a fallback board; Sharp Memory Display for a low-power status screen.
- Target user: an elderly relative or similar; the box reads letters aloud and flags bills and deadlines.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
1. No network at runtime. Prove it with a firewall drop rule and a packet capture.
2. No remote telemetry. Usage logs stay on the device and are shown to the user.
3. Test letters are used with the owner's consent; images and text are deleted after the study unless the owner says otherwise.
4. The box never pays, emails or acts; it reads, summarizes and flags, and says 'I am not sure' when OCR confidence or the summary is weak.
5. Every performance number is measured on the target board under a 30-minute soak, not a cold single run.

DELIVERABLES IN ORDER
1. stage1.md: Gemma Translator built as published, tokens per second, per-stage latency, temperature and throttle flags, deviations.
2. testset/: 20 letters, hand transcription, hand labels for bill, amount, due date, action, made by a second person.
3. pipeline/: capture, OCR, summarize, TTS, with per-stage timing and a confidence rule.
4. bench.md: p50 and p95 seconds per page, character error rate, bill-flag precision and recall, watts, peak temperature; Unlimited OCR versus a smaller fallback OCR if needed.
5. offline_proof/: nftables rules, tcpdump pcap, ss output, all from a full 20-letter run.
6. case/: modified STL or CadQuery source with camera mount, button, speaker grille, BOM with prices.
7. trial.md: two-week usage log summary and end interview.
8. verdict.md: falsifier result and GAPS.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
Write GAPS: models that did not fit in memory or ran too slowly and what replaced them; letter types missing from the test set (handwritten, multi-page, low light); thermal throttling events; claims not testable on this hardware (27B models, 100-page PDFs). Fill gaps you can, such as adding handwritten samples or rerunning with a heatsink change.

SELF-QUESTIONS
- Which stage dominates latency, and does quantization or a smaller OCR model fix it without wrecking accuracy?
- Does Unlimited OCR even run on a Pi 5's 8GB or 16GB RAM, or does this force a Jetson?
- What happens when the letter is crooked, folded, or in dim light?
- Does the summary ever invent an amount or date not in the OCR text?
- Is the voice clear to someone with hearing loss at the speaker's volume?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop and report if stage 1 cannot reach within 30% of the published 7 tokens per second, if p95 per page exceeds 30 s with every model option, or if the trial user declines.

RETURN FORMAT
Verdict line, bench table, offline proof summary, file list, GAPS, self-question answers.

steps.title: Ground truth: rebuild Gemma Translator as published
steps.goal: Learn the exact deployment path and limits of a Pi 5 running a three-model offline stack.
steps.prompt: Clone the Gemma Translator repository and follow its README and deployment script exactly on a Raspberry Pi 5 with the official active cooler and a 5V 5A supply. Record OS image, Python version, model files and their quantization, and every command. Do not change anything until the published build works. Then measure: tokens per second for Gemma during translation (compare to the published roughly 7), Moonshine latency per utterance, TTS real-time factor, and end-to-end latency from end of speech to start of playback, each over 20 utterances with p50 and p95. Run a 30-minute continuous soak and log vcgencmd measure_temp and get_throttled every 10 s, plus watts from a USB meter. Write stage1.md with results and every deviation from the repo's instructions, including missing steps you had to work out.
steps.expect: stage1.md with a command log, latency table, thermal and power plot, and a deviations list.
steps.audit: Fail if tokens per second is more than 30% below published without an explanation, or if get_throttled shows throttling you did not report. Fix cooling or power and rerun before step 2.

steps.title: Build the labeled letter test set
steps.goal: Create the ground truth the appliance will be judged on.
steps.prompt: With the owner's consent, collect 20 real letters representative of the target user's mail: utility bills, bank statements, medical appointment letters, government notices, marketing, and at least two handwritten or low-quality items. Photograph each with the same camera and stand planned for the device, and also under dim light and at a 15-degree tilt for a robustness subset. Have a second person, not the builder, hand-transcribe each letter and label: is it a bill (yes or no), amount due, due date, sender, and action needed. Store under testset/ with images, transcription text and labels.csv. Redact account numbers in any copy that leaves the device, and write a deletion date. Include at least one two-page letter so the pipeline's multi-page handling is tested.
steps.expect: testset/ with 20 letters, robustness variants, transcriptions and labels.csv, plus a consent and deletion note.
steps.audit: Fail if labels were made by the same person who builds the pipeline, or if bills are under 5 of 20, which makes recall meaningless. Add letters until both pass.

steps.title: Build the paperwork-reader pipeline
steps.goal: Fork the translator into capture, OCR, summarize, speak, with honest confidence.
steps.prompt: Fork the repo. Replace the speech input path with a camera capture on button press, with automatic crop and deskew in OpenCV. Run Baidu Unlimited OCR locally; if it does not fit RAM or exceeds 20 s per page on the Pi, benchmark a smaller OCR fallback and record both. Feed OCR text to quantized Gemma via llama.cpp with a fixed template: sender, what it is, amount, due date, action needed, confidence. Add a rule: if OCR mean confidence is low or any amount or date in the summary does not appear verbatim in the OCR text, the box says 'I am not sure about this letter, please ask someone to check it.' Speak the summary with Kyutai Pocket TTS at a slow rate. Time every stage with perf_counter and log locally.
steps.expect: pipeline/ code, config with model paths and quantization, and a per-stage timing log.
steps.audit: Feed three letters and check that every amount and date spoken appears in the OCR text. Fail on any invented value; tighten the verbatim-check rule and rerun.

steps.title: Benchmark accuracy, latency and offline proof
steps.goal: Measure the appliance against the labeled set with radios off.
steps.prompt: Add an nftables rule dropping all output except loopback, disable Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, and start tcpdump on all interfaces. Run all 20 letters plus robustness variants through the pipeline during a 30-minute soak. Compute: seconds per page p50 and p95 by stage; character error rate with jiwer against the transcriptions; bill-flag precision and recall, amount exact-match rate, and due-date exact-match rate against labels.csv; rate of 'not sure' responses and whether they landed on genuinely hard letters; peak temperature and throttle events; average watts. Stop tcpdump and confirm zero non-loopback packets; save the pcap and ss -tupn output in offline_proof/. Write bench.md comparing Unlimited OCR with the fallback if both ran. Break results out by letter type so weak categories are visible.
steps.expect: bench.md with tables per metric and offline_proof/ with pcap, firewall rules and socket list.
steps.audit: Fail if any non-loopback packet appears; find the process and remove it. Fail if a wrong amount was spoken without the 'not sure' warning; that is the highest-severity error.

steps.title: Case, BOM and two-week trial
steps.goal: Package it as a box a non-technical person can use, then watch real use.
steps.prompt: Modify the Gemma Translator STL or write a CadQuery case: camera on an arm over a letter tray, one large button, speaker grille facing the user, vents over the Pi's cooler, optional Sharp Memory Display for a status line. Write a BOM with part numbers and prices. Give the box to one non-technical person for two weeks with a one-page printed guide in large type. On the device, log locally: button presses, pages read, 'not sure' events, and replays. No remote telemetry. Observe the first use without helping and note where they hesitate. At the end, interview them: what they used it for, what annoyed them, whether they went back to a phone app or asking family, and when. Record the build time.
steps.expect: case/ files, BOM, trial.md with usage counts per day, first-use observations and interview notes.
steps.audit: Fail if the log shows the device was unused for more than 7 consecutive days without a recorded reason. Confirm consent and the deletion date for letter images captured during the trial.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Apply the falsifier and record what remains unproven.
steps.prompt: Write verdict.md. State p95 seconds per page against the roughly 10 s falsifier threshold, bill-flag recall and precision, amount accuracy, the offline proof result, and the trial outcome: did the person keep using it or revert to a phone app within a week? Give one verdict line: does the appliance form factor earn its keep at today's edge compute? Then GAPS: each source claim (7 tokens per second on Pi 5; weekend build from BOM; Unlimited OCR reads 100 pages in one pass; Pocket TTS 6x real time; 27B on one 24GB card; Soup on 4GB) marked verified, unverified or false on this hardware with the measurement that decides it; letter types not covered; failures during the trial. Recommend the single change most likely to fix the worst gap, such as a Jetson Orin Nano, a smaller OCR, or a better camera stand.
steps.expect: verdict.md with metrics, a verdict line and GAPS.
steps.audit: Recompute p95 and recall from the raw timing log and labels with a fresh script. Fail if any claim is marked verified without a number from this build.

offline-ai-appliances.gap_audit_prompt: You are an independent reviewer of an offline paperwork-reader appliance. Open stage1.md, testset/, pipeline/, bench.md, offline_proof/, case/, trial.md and verdict.md. List every claim in bench.md and verdict.md. Mark each verified (cite the log line, pcap, or computation), unverified (say what measurement would prove it), or false. Check: tokens per second and latency were measured under a 30-minute soak with throttle state recorded; labels were made by someone other than the builder; every spoken amount or date appears in OCR text, or triggered a 'not sure' warning; the pcap shows zero non-loopback packets during the full run; no remote telemetry exists in code; consent and deletion are documented for real letters; the trial outcome comes from the device log and interview, not the builder's impression. List missing pieces: untested letter types, models that never ran, robustness variants skipped. Rank problems by harm to the user first (a missed bill is worse than a slow page), then by whether they flip the falsifier verdict. Fix the top three now and report before and after. End with what needs new hardware, more letters, or a longer trial.
self_questions: Which stage dominates per-page latency on the Pi 5, and what is the cheapest fix?
Does Unlimited OCR fit and run in this board's RAM, or did I silently fall back?
Can the summary state an amount or date that is not in the OCR text, and did I test for it?
Is 'not sure' firing on the hard letters, or randomly?
Did any library phone home at import time (model hub checks, telemetry) and get caught by tcpdump?
Does the device throttle after 20 minutes in its printed case with the lid on?
Can the trial user hear and understand the TTS voice at the speaker's volume?
Are handwritten and multi-page letters represented in the test set?
What would make the person go back to a phone app, and did the log or interview show it?
