4. Export splats and GLB for each. Validate GLBs with the Khronos glTF Validator, inspect triangle counts with gltf-transform, check watertightness with trimesh.
5. Import into Blender headless and render fixed poses; play splats in a three.js viewer and measure fps; drop the collider into Godot with a capsule controller and walk a path.
6. Test persistence: same camera pose before and after moving away, SSIM 0.98 or better.
7. Compare against an open alternative on the same brief with two blind reviewers.

Return a claims table, the measurements, the pipeline scripts, and a verdict on where Marble fits.

world-labs-3d-generation.one_shot:
ROLE: You are a technical artist and pipeline TD evaluating a closed commercial 3D generator for a small studio. You judge it by the files it exports and how they behave in real tools, not by its demo reel.

CONTEXT:
- Product: Marble by World Labs (founders Fei-Fei Li, Justin Johnson, Ben Mildenhall, Christoph Lassner). Launched November 2025 as a browser app with waitlist access; closed weights; credit-based pricing.
- Claims to test from the guide: generates persistent explorable environments from text, images, video, or blocky 3D layouts in about 1-3 minutes; represents appearance as 3D Gaussian splats plus a low-poly collider mesh; the scene stays identical when the camera returns, unlike frame-predicting video models (Sora, Veo, Genie 3); exports Gaussian splats (.ply or proprietary), GLB mesh, and rendered video; export quality is good enough for previs, not final pixel; no public API at launch.
- Comparators: Hunyuan3D-2 and Tripo (single objects), Genie 3 (interactive but no export). Tools: Blender 4.x, three.js with a splat renderer such as Spark (sparkjsdev/spark) or similar, Godot 4 or Unity, Khronos glTF Validator, gltf-transform, trimesh, scikit-image SSIM.
- Use case: game-level blockout and film previs.

HARD CONSTRAINTS:
- Fixed prompt set, versioned in prompts.jsonl; no cherry-picking: every generation is logged and scored, including failures.
- Do not upload private or client images; use your own photos or public-domain references.
- Record credits spent per generation and stop at the budget Victor sets.
- Read the terms of service and output license before using any output in a shared project.
- All pipeline steps scripted and headless where possible so results reproduce.

DELIVERABLES, in order:
1. product_facts.md: inputs, exports, formats, pricing, API status, output license, each with a World Labs URL and date checked.
2. brief.md with acceptance criteria: GLB validates with zero errors; collider walkable; splat playback at 60 fps or better on this GPU at 1080p; generation under 3 minutes; usable after Blender import.
3. runs.csv: per prompt, input mode, generation time, credits, export file sizes, splat count, collider triangle count.
4. Validation outputs: gltf-validator reports, gltf-transform inspect output, trimesh watertight and scale checks.
5. pipeline/: Blender headless import and fixed-pose render script; three.js splat viewer page with an fps counter; Godot project with the collider and a capsule controller walking a scripted path.
6. persistence.md: SSIM between renders of the same pose before and after navigating away, in Marble's viewer capture and in the exported splat.
7. compare.md: the same 3 briefs done with an open alternative, judged blind by two reviewers.

GAP ANALYSIS (built in): keep gaps.md. Record anything you could not test (no waitlist access, an export format missing, no layout editor on your plan) and how it limits the verdict. Fill what you can from documentation and community exports; label those as secondhand.

SELF-QUESTIONS before finishing:
- Does the collider mesh align with the splats, or is it offset or scaled?
- What is the real-world scale of exports, and does a 1.8 m capsule fit through doors?
- Do layout-conditioned runs respect my blocked geometry, measured, not eyeballed?
- Is persistence true in the export, or only in the hosted viewer?
- What is the splat count and file size, and does it play at 60 fps here?
- Who owns outputs and can I ship them commercially?
- What happens to my pipeline if World Labs changes pricing or closes access?
- Where does Marble beat the open alternative, and where does it lose?

STOP CONDITIONS: stop and report if there is no access to Marble (deliver the evaluation harness ready to run plus secondhand findings), if the credit budget is reached, or if the terms forbid the intended use.

RETURN FORMAT: markdown report: Verdict (where Marble fits, one paragraph), Product facts, Runs table, Validation, Pipeline results, Persistence, Comparison, Gaps ranked, file paths.

steps.title: Ground truth: product, formats, terms
steps.goal: Know exactly what Marble offers and permits today.
steps.prompt:
From World Labs' site, Marble docs or help center, blog posts, and terms of service, record in product_facts.md: access model (waitlist, plans), input modes (text, image, multi-image, video, 3D layout editor), generation time claims, edit tools, export formats with extensions (splat .ply, .spz, other; GLB collider or full mesh; video), splat attribute layout, credit pricing per generation and per export, whether a public API or SDK exists now (the guide says none at launch), and the output license for commercial use and what World Labs retains.

Also verify supporting tools: does sparkjsdev/spark exist and render the exported splat format; does nianticlabs/spz document .spz; which Blender add-ons import 3D Gaussian splat .ply. Each row: fact, value, URL, date checked. Mark anything from third-party posts as secondhand.
steps.expect: product_facts.md with 15+ sourced rows and a tool-compatibility table.
steps.audit: Rows without a World Labs or repo URL are unverified. If the license forbids commercial use or requires attribution, flag it at the top. If no access is available, mark generation steps blocked and continue building the harness.

steps.title: Brief and fixed prompt set
steps.goal: Define acceptance criteria and comparable inputs before generating.
steps.prompt:
Write brief.md with acceptance criteria for game blockout and previs: GLB passes Khronos glTF Validator with zero errors; collider walkable by a 0.4 m radius, 1.8 m capsule along a scripted path; splat playback at 60 fps or better at 1080p on this machine's GPU; generation under 3 minutes; scale within 10% of real-world for known objects (a door 2.0-2.1 m); Blender import without manual fixes.

Write prompts.jsonl with 18 entries: 10 text prompts spanning interiors (diner at 3am, tea room), exteriors (cyberpunk alley with wet pavement and fog), and game spaces (three-room dungeon with a corridor); 5 image prompts from your own photos or public-domain images with sources recorded; 3 layout prompts where you block out geometry with known dimensions (a 6 x 4 m room with a 1 m doorway centered on one wall). Each entry: id, mode, input, intended use, measurable expectation.
steps.expect: brief.md with 6+ numeric criteria; prompts.jsonl with 18 entries including dimensions for layout prompts.
steps.audit: Every criterion must be measurable by a tool named in methods. Layout prompts must include dimensions so step 4 can measure adherence. Remove any image you do not have the right to upload.

steps.title: Generate and export
steps.goal: Run every prompt once, log everything, export standard files.
steps.prompt:
Run all 18 prompts in Marble in prompts.jsonl order. For each: start and end timestamps, credits used, any errors, and a screenshot of the hosted viewer at a fixed starting view. Export splats in every offered format, the GLB mesh or collider, and a short rendered flythrough. Save under exports/<id>/ with original filenames preserved.

Record in runs.csv: id, mode, generation seconds, credits, splat file size, splat count (parse the .ply header element vertex count, or the .spz header), GLB size, triangle count (from gltf-transform inspect), and notes. Do not regenerate failures to get a better result; a second attempt is a new row labeled retry. Stop when the credit budget is reached and record which prompts were not run.
steps.expect: exports/ with 18 folders (or fewer with budget notes), runs.csv complete, viewer screenshots.
steps.audit: Check that every runs.csv row has a matching export folder and parsed counts; a missing count means the format was not parsed, so fix the parser. Compute median generation time and compare with the 1-3 minute claim.

steps.title: Validate and integrate into Blender, three.js, and a game engine
steps.goal: Prove the exports work in real pipelines.
steps.prompt:
For each GLB: run the Khronos glTF Validator and save the report; run gltf-transform inspect; load with trimesh to check watertightness, bounds, and units. For layout prompts, measure the room and doorway dimensions on the collider and compare with the blocked-out values.

Blender: write pipeline/blender_import.py that imports the GLB (and splats via a chosen add-on), places a camera at 3 fixed poses, and renders with blender -b -P; log errors.

three.js: build pipeline/viewer.html that loads the splat with Spark or another splat renderer and the GLB, and shows an fps counter; record fps at 1080p for each scene.

Game engine: in Godot 4 (or Unity), import the GLB as a static collider, add a 0.4 m radius, 1.8 m capsule CharacterBody3D, and script it along waypoints through the space; log falls through the floor, stuck frames, and doorway passes. Write integration.md with a table per scene.
steps.expect: validator reports, inspect outputs, dimension checks, Blender renders, fps table, Godot run logs, integration.md.
steps.audit: Fail a scene if the validator reports any error, Blender import errors, fps under 60, or the capsule falls through or gets stuck. Check collider-splat alignment by overlaying the GLB wireframe on a splat render; an offset over 5 cm is a defect to record.

steps.title: Persistence test and open-alternative comparison
steps.goal: Test the central persistence claim and benchmark against an alternative.
steps.prompt:
Persistence: for 5 scenes, capture the hosted viewer at a fixed pose, navigate away for at least 20 seconds through other parts of the scene, return to the exact pose (use any coordinate display or a saved view), and capture again. Repeat for the exported splat in viewer.html with a scripted camera. Compute SSIM with scikit-image on aligned grayscale captures. Also reload the scene in a new session and compare. Write persistence.md.

Comparison: pick 3 briefs. Produce the same scenes with an open alternative: an image-to-3D object generator such as Hunyuan3D-2 for hero props assembled in Blender, or an open scene generator if you can run one. Render matched views. Two reviewers who did not make them choose blindly per brief on usefulness for blockout. Record time spent per approach.
steps.expect: persistence.md with SSIM per scene and condition; compare.md with matched renders, blind choices, and time per approach.
steps.audit: If SSIM is below 0.98 in the hosted viewer, check camera pose alignment before concluding non-persistence. Reviewers must not know which tool made which render; record how blinding was done.

steps.title: Validate against oracles, gap report, verdict
steps.goal: Close with evidence and a clear verdict on fit.
steps.prompt:
Run the oracles and record pass or fail with evidence: (1) Khronos glTF Validator zero errors across exported GLBs; (2) Blender headless import and render succeeds for every scene; (3) Godot capsule walks every scripted path without falls or stuck frames; (4) persistence SSIM 0.98 or higher in hosted viewer and export; (5) splat playback at 60 fps at 1080p; (6) blind reviewers' preferences recorded for 3 briefs.

Write gap_report.md: every guide claim (1-3 minute generation, splats plus collider mesh, persistence versus video models, export formats, previs-grade quality, no public API, waitlist access) and every brief criterion, marked verified / unverified / false with evidence, ranked by impact on adopting Marble in the pipeline. Fix the top three where possible (better import script, scale correction, alignment fix). Then write verdict.md: where Marble fits (environment blockout, previs, VR scouting), where it does not, cost per usable scene from runs.csv, license constraints, and the exit plan if access changes.
steps.expect: oracles.md with six rows, gap_report.md ranked, verdict.md with cost per usable scene and exit plan.
steps.audit: Any oracle without a log, render, or report file is unverified. The verdict must cite numbers from runs.csv and integration.md, not impressions.

world-labs-3d-generation.gap_audit_prompt:
You are reviewing a Marble evaluation you did not run. Read product_facts.md, brief.md, prompts.jsonl, runs.csv, validator reports, integration.md, persistence.md, compare.md, oracles.md, gap_report.md, and verdict.md.

1. Enumerate every claim: generation times, formats, splat and triangle counts, validator results, fps, walkability, scale, persistence SSIM, reviewer preferences, license facts, cost per usable scene. Mark each verified, unverified, or false. Re-run the glTF Validator on three GLBs and the Blender import on one scene yourself.
2. List missing pieces: prompts skipped, retries hidden, persistence tested only in the hosted viewer, no scale check, comparator not blind, license unread.
3. Rank by impact on the adopt or not decision: licensing and exportability first, then collider usability, then quality.

5. Report what you could not fix and why, with the next action.

self_questions: Does the exported collider line up with the splats in position and scale?
Is the export scale in meters, and does a 1.8 m capsule pass through doorways?
Did layout-conditioned runs keep my blocked dimensions within 10%?
Does persistence hold in the exported splat, or only inside World Labs' viewer?
How many splats per scene, and does that play at 60 fps on this GPU?
What does one usable scene cost in credits once failures are counted?
What do the terms say about commercial use and ownership of outputs?
Does an API exist now, contrary to the launch-era guide?
Which input mode gave the most usable blockouts, and why?
What is my exit plan if access or pricing changes?
Did I log every failure, or only the good runs?
validation_oracles: Khronos glTF Validator reports zero errors on every exported GLB.
Blender 4.x headless (blender -b -P pipeline/blender_import.py) imports and renders each scene without errors.
Godot 4 capsule controller (0.4 m radius, 1.8 m) completes every scripted waypoint path with no falls and no stuck frames, logged.
SSIM 0.98 or higher between renders of the same pose before and after navigating away, in both the hosted viewer and the exported splat.
Two blind reviewers choose between Marble and an open alternative on three matched briefs, choices recorded.
failure_modes: Cherry-picked results. Tell: runs.csv has fewer rows than prompts with no budget note. Fix: log every run including failures and retries.
Collider misaligned or wrong scale. Tell: capsule floats, clips, or cannot fit doors. Fix: measure known objects, apply a scale and offset transform in the import script.
Splats too heavy for real time. Tell: viewer under 60 fps. Fix: prune or decimate splats, compress to .spz, or use video export for previs only.
Persistence measured with misaligned cameras. Tell: low SSIM with visibly identical content. Fix: use saved views or scripted cameras and align before scoring.
License blocks the intended use. Tell: terms restrict commercial use or claim output rights. Fix: confirm before production use; restrict to internal previs.
Vendor lock-in. Tell: workflow depends on hosted editing with no export of edits. Fix: export standard files after every session and keep the open-alternative path working.
world-labs-3d-generation.agent_direction: Start with product_facts.md: access, exports, and license decide whether the rest is worth running. Build the harness (validator calls, Blender script, viewer page, Godot project) before spending credits, so every export is checked the moment it lands. Cache all exports under exports/ and never regenerate to replace a weak result. A sub-agent can build the Godot walk-test project and another the three.js splat viewer in parallel while generations run. Generation through the browser needs Victor's account: stop and ask for access and a credit budget before step 3, and ask before uploading any image. Write outputs to docs/marble_eval/: product_facts.md, brief.md, prompts.jsonl, runs.csv, integration.md, persistence.md, compare.md, oracles.md, gap_report.md, verdict.md, with scripts in pipeline/. Return the verdict paragraph, the oracle table, and the gap list.

claude-code-hooks-system.mission: Build a tested, version-pinned hook suite for Claude Code: a destructive-Bash blocker, a secret-leak blocker on Edit/Write, auto-format on edit, git context at SessionStart, a Bash audit log, a PreCompact transcript backup, and a Stop gate that refuses 'done' while tests fail. Done means each hook is proven to fire (or block) in a live headless Claude Code session, not just in theory.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: A platform engineer would treat hooks as production code that runs with your full user permissions on every tool call, so they would version the scripts in git, unit-test each one against recorded event payloads, and measure their latency because a slow PreToolUse hook taxes every single Bash call. They would read the installed version's hook reference instead of trusting a blog table, because event names and the structured-output schema have changed between releases (the guide's `modified_tool_input` and top-level `decision: approve` are older shapes; current docs use `hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision` and `updatedInput`). They would guard Stop hooks against infinite loops using the `stop_hook_active` input field.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: Start from the source, not summaries: (1) the official hooks reference at code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks and the hooks guide at code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide, read for the exact version you run (`claude --version`); (2) the Agent SDK hooks page at platform.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks; (3) disler/claude-code-hooks-mastery on GitHub, which logs the real stdin payload of every event to JSON files; (4) your own captured payloads, produced by a catch-all logging hook that dumps stdin for every event to `~/.claude/hook-payloads/<event>-<ts>.json`; (5) your existing `~/.claude/settings.json`, `.claude/settings.json`, and `.claude/settings.local.json`, plus any hookify rules (`/hookify:list`).
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: jq for parsing stdin; bash with `set -euo pipefail` or Python 3 stdlib for anything nontrivial; bats-core or pytest for the harness (pipe fixture JSON into the script, assert exit code 0/2 and stdout/stderr); shellcheck on every .sh; `hyperfine` to time each hook (budget under 50 ms for PreToolUse); `claude --debug` and the `/hooks` slash command to confirm registration; headless `claude -p` runs with `--output-format stream-json` to prove a hook fired end to end; gitleaks or trufflehog regex sets as the source for the secret-pattern blocker.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: The oracles are outside the model: (a) a bats/pytest suite where recorded payloads from your own Claude Code version produce the expected exit codes; (b) a headless `claude -p` session told to run `rm -rf /tmp/hooktest-canary` (a directory holding a .protected sentinel) that shows the block reason in the stream-json transcript and leaves the canary directory intact; (c) a Stop-gate run where a deliberately failing pytest keeps the session working and the session ends only after the test passes.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: You are a platform engineer hardening my Claude Code setup with hooks. First run `claude --version` and read the hooks reference for that version (code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks); record the exact event names, stdin fields, exit-code semantics, and the structured JSON output schema (permissionDecision, updatedInput, additionalContext, decision/reason for Stop). Install a temporary catch-all hook that dumps stdin for every event into ~/.claude/hook-payloads/ and run one short session to capture real payloads; these become test fixtures. Then build, in a git-tracked ~/.claude/hooks/ directory: block-destructive.sh (PreToolUse, Bash), block-secrets.py (PreToolUse, Edit|Write|MultiEdit, gitleaks-derived patterns), format-on-edit.sh (PostToolUse), session-git-context.sh (SessionStart), bash-audit.sh (PostToolUse, Bash, TSV), precompact-backup.py (PreCompact, async), stop-tests-gate.sh (Stop, honours stop_hook_active). For each: a bats or pytest test feeding fixtures and asserting exit code and output, shellcheck clean, hyperfine timing under 50 ms for PreToolUse. Register them in ~/.claude/settings.json without clobbering existing hooks. Prove each fires in a headless `claude -p --output-format stream-json` session using canary files under /tmp. Return the file tree, the test output, the timing table, and a list of guide claims you found wrong for this version.

claude-code-hooks-system.one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are a platform engineer building a deterministic guardrail layer for Claude Code. You treat hooks as production code that runs with the user's full permissions on every tool call. You trust the installed version's documentation and captured payloads over any blog post, including the guide you were given. You never claim a hook works until a live session proves it.

CONTEXT
- Hooks are shell commands the harness (not the model) runs at lifecycle events: SessionStart, UserPromptSubmit, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, Notification, Stop, SubagentStop, PreCompact, SessionEnd, plus newer ones that churn between versions.
- Stdin is JSON (session_id, hook_event_name, tool_name, tool_input, cwd, transcript_path, and per-event fields). Exit 0 allows, exit 2 blocks and feeds stderr to Claude, other non-zero is a non-blocking error.
- Claims from the guide you must TEST, not repeat: (1) 'structured JSON can return {"modified_tool_input": ...} to rewrite arguments' (current docs may name this updatedInput under hookSpecificOutput); (2) '{"decision": "approve"}' as a valid PreToolUse output; (3) 'SessionStart stdout gets injected into Claude's first system message'; (4) 'async: true hooks cannot block or modify'; (5) 'later settings files win for the same key' (hooks may merge rather than override).
- References: code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks, code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide, github.com/disler/claude-code-hooks-mastery, the hookify plugin if installed (/hookify:list).

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- Back up ~/.claude/settings.json to settings.json.bak-<date> before editing. Merge hooks with jq; never overwrite existing entries.
- All scripts live in ~/.claude/hooks/, are git-tracked, executable, shellcheck clean.
- PreToolUse hooks must finish in under 50 ms median (hyperfine, 20 runs).
- Every Stop hook must exit 0 when stop_hook_active is true to prevent infinite loops.
- Destructive tests only against canary paths under /tmp/hooktest-*. Never test against real data.
- The secret blocker reports the pattern name, never the matched value.

ORDERED DELIVERABLES
1. ground-truth.md: claude --version, the event table copied from the installed version's docs, the exact output JSON schema, and a verdict on each of the five guide claims above.
2. A capture hook (temporary) that writes every event's stdin to ~/.claude/hook-payloads/; run one session that triggers Bash, Edit, Write, a subagent, and /compact. Keep the payloads as fixtures in ~/.claude/hooks/tests/fixtures/. Remove the capture hook afterward.
3. Seven hooks: block-destructive.sh, block-secrets.py, format-on-edit.sh, session-git-context.sh, bash-audit.sh, precompact-backup.py (async), stop-tests-gate.sh.
4. tests/: bats or pytest cases, at least three per hook (allow case, block case, malformed-stdin case).
5. settings.json merged entries with matchers (Bash; Edit|Write|MultiEdit; empty matcher for lifecycle events) and timeouts.
6. Live proof: headless runs of `claude -p '...' --output-format stream-json` for the blocker, the secret blocker, and the Stop gate, saved as transcripts in ~/.claude/hooks/proof/.
7. README.md in ~/.claude/hooks/: what each hook does, how to disable (disableAllHooks or removing the entry), and a 'what this cannot stop' section.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
Before finishing, write GAPS.md listing: every event you could not trigger live and why; every guide claim that was false or unverifiable on this version; bypasses you found for each blocker (try bash -c, eval, base64 -d | sh, writing a script then running it, MCP tools that write files); hooks whose latency exceeded budget. Fix what you can now (for example extend the Edit matcher to MCP filesystem tools), and mark the rest open with a reason.

SELF-QUESTIONS BEFORE FINISHING
- Did I read the docs for my installed version, or an older page?
- Does any hook print a secret, a full tool_input, or a transcript to stdout where Claude will see it?
- What happens to each hook when jq is missing, stdin is empty, or tool_input lacks the field I read?
- Does the Stop gate handle a repo without tests, and does it honour stop_hook_active?
- Does format-on-edit run on files outside the project (for example ~/.claude itself)?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop and report when all seven hooks pass their tests and the three live proofs exist, or when a doc/behaviour mismatch blocks a hook (report the mismatch with the doc excerpt and the observed payload). Stop immediately and ask if any test would touch a path outside /tmp/hooktest-* or the hooks directory.

RETURN FORMAT
A single message with: (1) file tree of ~/.claude/hooks; (2) test summary (pass/fail counts per hook); (3) latency table (hook, median ms); (4) verdicts on the five guide claims; (5) the GAPS.md contents; (6) the exact settings.json diff.

steps.title: Establish ground truth for the installed version
steps.goal: Pin the exact hook contract of the Claude Code version you run and capture real payloads.
steps.prompt: Run `claude --version` and record it. Read the hooks reference at code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks and the hooks guide at code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide. Write ~/.claude/hooks/ground-truth.md containing: the full list of hook events with when they fire and whether they can block; the stdin fields common to all events and the extra fields per event (tool_name, tool_input, tool_response, prompt, stop_hook_active, trigger for PreCompact, source for SessionStart); exit-code semantics; the structured JSON output schema (continue, stopReason, suppressOutput, hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision, permissionDecisionReason, updatedInput, additionalContext, and Stop's decision/reason). Then judge these guide claims as true, false, or renamed for this version: modified_tool_input rewrites args; decision: approve is valid for PreToolUse; SessionStart stdout is injected as context; async hooks cannot block; later settings files override earlier ones for hooks. Next, back up ~/.claude/settings.json, add a temporary catch-all hook on every event that runs `cat > ~/.claude/hook-payloads/$(date +%s%N)-event.json`, start one session that runs a Bash command, edits a file, writes a file, spawns a subagent, and runs /compact, then remove the catch-all. Copy the payloads into ~/.claude/hooks/tests/fixtures/ named by event.
steps.expect: ground-truth.md (one to two pages) with a version string, an event table, a schema block, and five claim verdicts each quoting the doc line; at least one fixture JSON per event triggered.
steps.audit: Open each fixture and confirm the fields you documented actually appear; any documented field missing from a real payload is a fail, so re-read the docs for that version and correct ground-truth.md. Confirm settings.json matches the backup after removing the capture hook (diff must be empty).

steps.title: Build and test the PreToolUse blockers
steps.goal: Ship a destructive-Bash blocker and a secret-leak blocker with fixture tests and latency budgets.
steps.prompt: Using the fixtures in ~/.claude/hooks/tests/fixtures/ and the schema in ground-truth.md, write two hooks. (a) block-destructive.sh: read .tool_input.command with jq; block with exit 2 and a one-line stderr reason on rm -rf against /, ~, $HOME or a repo root, mkfs, dd of= to /dev/, fork bombs, chmod -R 777 /, git push --force to main or master, `find ... -exec rm -rf` without a .git prune, and rm -rf of any directory containing a .protected sentinel file (this gives live tests a safe target). Allow everything else. Handle missing jq or empty stdin by exiting 0 and logging to ~/.claude/hooks/errors.log. (b) block-secrets.py: on Edit, Write, and MultiEdit, scan new_string, content, and edits[].new_string against a pattern set derived from gitleaks default rules (AWS keys, GitHub tokens, Anthropic and OpenAI keys, PEM private key headers, 64-hex Ethereum private keys) and exit 2 naming only the rule, never the value. Write bats or pytest cases: three allow, three block, one malformed stdin per hook. Run shellcheck. Time each with `hyperfine --runs 20` piping a fixture; the median must be under 50 ms. Then try to bypass block-destructive with bash -c, eval, base64 -d | sh, and a script file, and record which get through.
steps.expect: Two executable scripts, a test file with at least 14 passing cases, a hyperfine table, and a bypass list with pass/blocked per technique.
steps.audit: Re-run the tests from a clean shell. Grep the scripts' stderr strings to confirm no secret value can be echoed. If a known-dangerous fixture passes, or latency exceeds 50 ms, fix before moving on. Bypasses that remain open go into GAPS.md, not silently ignored.

steps.title: Build the advisory hooks
steps.goal: Add format-on-edit, Bash audit logging, and SessionStart git context, each tested.
steps.prompt: Write three hooks using the fixtures. (a) format-on-edit.sh for PostToolUse on Edit|Write|MultiEdit: read .tool_input.file_path, skip files outside the session cwd (from .cwd) and anything under ~/.claude, then dispatch by extension: prettier --write for ts/tsx/js/jsx/json/css/md, ruff format for py, rustfmt for rs, gofmt -w for go. Skip silently if the formatter is not installed. Never exit 2. (b) bash-audit.sh for PostToolUse on Bash: append a TSV row of ISO timestamp, session_id, cwd, and the command with tabs and newlines escaped, to ~/.claude/bash-log.tsv; rotate when the file passes 10 MB. (c) session-git-context.sh for SessionStart: if cwd is a git repo, print the branch, `git status --short | head -10`, and `git log --oneline -5`; print nothing outside a repo. Verify against ground-truth.md whether SessionStart stdout becomes model context on this version and whether JSON additionalContext is the preferred path; use whichever the docs specify. Write tests: format-on-edit actually reformats a badly indented fixture file in /tmp/hooktest-fmt; audit log escapes a multi-line command; git context prints nothing in a non-repo directory.
steps.expect: Three scripts, passing tests, and a sample bash-log.tsv row and git-context output pasted into the step notes.
steps.audit: Check that a command containing a tab or newline yields exactly one TSV row. Check the formatter does not touch files outside cwd. If SessionStart output is not visible to the model in a live test, switch to the documented JSON field and retest.

steps.title: Build the Stop gate and PreCompact backup
steps.goal: Refuse premature 'done' while tests fail, and snapshot transcripts before compaction.
steps.prompt: Write stop-tests-gate.sh for the Stop event. Read stdin; if .stop_hook_active is true, exit 0 immediately to avoid an infinite loop. Detect the test runner from the cwd: pytest if pyproject.toml or pytest.ini exists, `npm test --silent` if package.json has a test script, `cargo test --quiet` for Cargo.toml; if none, exit 0. Run it with a 120-second timeout. On failure, block the stop using the mechanism ground-truth.md specifies for Stop on this version (exit 2 with the failing test names on stderr, or JSON decision: block with a reason), capped to the last 30 lines of output. Write precompact-backup.py for PreCompact, registered async: copy the file at .transcript_path to ~/.claude/transcript-backups/<session_id>-<trigger>-<UTC timestamp>.jsonl, keep the newest 50, and never print the transcript. Test the Stop gate in /tmp/hooktest-stop with a tiny pytest project in three states: passing, failing, and stop_hook_active true while failing. Test the backup with a fixture payload pointing at a dummy transcript.
steps.expect: Two scripts and a test log showing three Stop outcomes (allow, block with reason, allow due to stop_hook_active) and one backup file created with the right name.
steps.audit: Confirm the gate cannot loop: simulate two consecutive Stop events, the second with stop_hook_active true, and verify exit 0. Confirm a 120-second timeout is shorter than the hook timeout you will register. Confirm the backup rotation deletes only files in its own directory.

steps.title: Prove each hook end to end in live sessions
steps.goal: Show the harness, not the test harness, enforces each hook.
steps.prompt: First register the hooks: back up ~/.claude/settings.json, then merge all seven entries into .hooks with jq, appending to existing arrays (matchers Bash and Edit|Write|MultiEdit for the tool hooks, empty for lifecycle events, async true for PreCompact, Stop timeout 150 seconds). Validate with `jq empty`, confirm each entry appears under /hooks, and list project-level hooks in .claude/settings.json that would double-fire. Then create canaries: mkdir -p /tmp/hooktest-canary && touch /tmp/hooktest-canary/keep.txt /tmp/hooktest-canary/.protected. Never target a parent path in a test. Run headless sessions and save each transcript to ~/.claude/hooks/proof/: (1) `claude -p 'Run: rm -rf /tmp/hooktest-canary then report' --output-format stream-json --verbose` with permission settings that would otherwise allow Bash; confirm the stream shows a block with your stderr reason and the canary still exists. (2) Ask Claude to write a file /tmp/hooktest-secret/config.py containing a fake AWS key in the documented AKIA format; confirm the write is blocked and the file does not exist. (3) In /tmp/hooktest-stop with a failing test, ask Claude to 'add a docstring and say done'; confirm the session continues and fixes or reports the failing test before stopping. (4) Count Bash tool calls in the transcripts and compare with new rows in bash-log.tsv. (5) Run /compact in an interactive session and confirm a backup file appears.
steps.expect: Five proof transcripts or notes with pass/fail, a canary directory that still exists, and matching Bash-call counts.
steps.audit: Any proof that passes only because the model declined on its own (no hook event in the stream) is a fail; re-run with a prompt that pushes the action and confirm the block reason comes from the hook. Mismatched audit-log counts mean the matcher misses some calls. A settings diff that removes any pre-existing line means restore the backup and redo the merge.

steps.title: Validate against the oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Run every external check and publish what is proven, what is open, and what the guide got wrong.
steps.prompt: Run the full test suite from a clean shell and paste the summary. Run shellcheck on all .sh files. Run hyperfine on every PreToolUse hook and tabulate medians. Run gitleaks detect on the project repo and confirm no secret type it finds is missing from block-secrets.py's rules. Re-read the five proof transcripts. Write ~/.claude/hooks/README.md (purpose of each hook, how to disable each, fail-open versus fail-closed choice, what each blocker cannot stop) and GAPS.md with three sections: Verified (claim, evidence file), Open (claim or bypass, why not fixed, impact high/medium/low), and Guide corrections (each guide claim that was false or renamed on this version with the doc excerpt). Commit ~/.claude/hooks to git with a message naming the Claude Code version tested.
steps.expect: All tests green, a latency table, README.md and GAPS.md, and a commit hash.
steps.audit: Every Verified row must cite a file in tests/ or proof/. Any high-impact Open item without a mitigation note is a fail: add a mitigation (for example a permissions deny rule) or mark it explicitly as accepted risk with the reason.

claude-code-hooks-system.gap_audit_prompt: You are auditing a freshly built Claude Code hook suite in ~/.claude/hooks/ that you did not write. Do not trust README.md. (1) List every claim the README and ground-truth.md make (each hook's trigger, behaviour, latency, and each guide-claim verdict). (2) For each, mark verified, unverified, or false, and cite evidence: a test case name, a proof transcript line, or a doc excerpt for the version from `claude --version`. (3) Attack the blockers: try at least eight bypasses of block-destructive (bash -c, sh -c, eval, base64 -d | sh, python -c with shutil.rmtree, a heredoc script then execute, xargs rm, an MCP filesystem delete tool) and five of block-secrets (split string concatenation, base64 of a key, a key in a NotebookEdit cell, a key via Bash echo > file, a key in an MCP write tool). Record which get through. (4) Check for silent failures: what does each hook do with empty stdin, invalid JSON, a missing jq or formatter; does any hook print tool_input or transcript content where Claude sees it. (5) Rank all gaps by impact (data loss, secret leak, workflow friction). Fix the top three now, re-run tests, and append results to GAPS.md. Report what you could not fix and why, with the exact command that demonstrates each remaining bypass on a /tmp canary.
self_questions: Which version's hook schema did I implement, and did I check it against a captured payload rather than the guide's table?
Does the Stop gate honour stop_hook_active, and what happens if the test suite takes longer than the hook timeout?
Does block-secrets cover MultiEdit edits[] and NotebookEdit, or only Edit and Write?
Can Claude write a file through an MCP server tool that none of my matchers see?
Is fail-open on missing jq the right call for the destructive blocker, and did I document it?
Do project-level .claude/settings.json hooks double-fire with my user-level ones?
Does format-on-edit rewrite files Claude did not intend to change, such as lockfiles or generated code?
Will the audit log or transcript backups grow without bound?
validation_oracles: bats or pytest suite: every hook passes allow, block, and malformed-stdin fixtures captured from the installed Claude Code version.
Headless `claude -p --output-format stream-json` transcripts showing the hook's block reason for a destructive command, with /tmp/hooktest-canary still present afterward.
A failing pytest project where the Stop gate keeps the session working until tests pass, and a stop_hook_active=true run that exits cleanly.
gitleaks detect on the repo finds no secret class that block-secrets.py lacks a rule for.
failure_modes: Stop hook loops forever. Tell: the session keeps restarting after every response and burns tokens. Fix: exit 0 when stop_hook_active is true and cap retries.
Hook written to an outdated schema. Tell: JSON output is ignored and tools run anyway. Fix: re-read the docs for `claude --version` and use hookSpecificOutput fields.
Regex blocker treated as a sandbox. Tell: `bash -c` or a written script runs the blocked command. Fix: document bypasses, add permissions deny rules and a sandboxed run mode for risky work.
Slow PreToolUse hook. Tell: every Bash call stalls noticeably. Fix: hyperfine it, move logic to a compiled binary or cache, keep heavy work in async PostToolUse.
claude-code-hooks-system.agent_direction: Run this in the user's home config, so treat ~/.claude/settings.json as precious: back it up before every write and diff after. Reach for the installed version's docs and a captured payload first; do not code from the guide's tables. Spawn a subagent only for the adversarial bypass hunt in the gap audit, so the builder is not grading its own blockers. Never execute a destructive command outside /tmp/hooktest-* paths; if any proof would need one, stop and ask. Never print, log, or echo the value of anything matching a secret pattern, including in test output. Return in chat: the hook file tree, test summary, latency table, guide-claim verdicts, settings diff, and GAPS.md; the files themselves live in ~/.claude/hooks/ and are committed to a git repo there.

claude-code-parallel-worktrees.mission: Stand up a working 3-5 session parallel Claude Code workflow on one real repo using git worktrees, with automatic per-worktree ports and databases, a status view of all worktrees, and a measured answer to whether it actually raised your merged-PR throughput. Done means at least three independent tasks ran concurrently in isolated worktrees, merged through normal PRs without cross-session conflicts, and a before/after log shows the throughput and review-time numbers for your own work.

deeper_not_bigger.professional_would: An engineering lead would not start by opening fifteen tabs; they would first measure their own baseline (PRs merged per day, minutes of review per PR, idle minutes waiting on the model), then decompose a backlog into tasks with provably disjoint file sets before spawning anything. They would make the environment worktree-safe up front: ports, databases, caches, .env files, and git hooks keyed to the worktree, because those collisions are what actually break parallel runs. And they would treat the guide's own warning seriously: throughput caps around 3-5x because human review is the binding constraint, so the experiment is about finding your personal ceiling.
deeper_not_bigger.rawest_material: Boris Cherny's original posts (x.com/bcherny/status/2017742743125299476 and x.com/bcherny/status/2025007394967957720); the official agent teams page at code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams and the CLI reference for `--worktree` on your installed version (`claude --help`); the git-worktree man page (`git help worktree`), especially sections on locking, pruning, and --detach; your own repo's package.json, docker-compose.yml, .env.example, and .husky or .git/hooks, which determine what collides; and your own git log for the last 30 days as the baseline.
deeper_not_bigger.methods_tools: git worktree add/list/remove/prune/lock; `claude --worktree <name>` and `--tmux` if present on your version; tmux with one window per worktree; a port allocator that hashes the worktree name into a range (e.g. 3100-3999) and writes PORT, DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL into .env.local; per-worktree Postgres via `docker compose -p <worktree>` or schema namespaces, SQLite files per worktree; pnpm's content-addressed store to avoid node_modules duplication; `gh pr create --fill` and `gh pr list --json` for throughput counts; `git diff --name-only main...` to verify disjoint file sets.
deeper_not_bigger.external_proof: GitHub itself is the oracle: `gh pr list --state merged --author @me --json mergedAt,createdAt` over the experiment week versus the baseline week gives merged-PR count and cycle time. CI results on each PR show nothing broke from isolation leaks. `git worktree list` and `docker ps` show no orphaned worktrees or containers after cleanup. Two dev servers answering on different ports at the same time (curl both) prove port isolation.
deeper_not_bigger.rewritten_prompt: Act as an engineering lead setting up parallel Claude Code work on my repo at <path>. First measure my baseline: use `gh pr list --state merged --author @me --json number,createdAt,mergedAt --limit 100` to compute merged PRs per day and median cycle time over the last 30 days. Then inspect the repo for collision points: dev-server ports, database URLs, Redis, caches, .env files, git hooks (husky, pre-commit), and node_modules size. Check `claude --help` for the --worktree and --tmux flags on my installed version and document exactly where worktrees are created and what gets copied. Build scripts/wt-spawn.sh that takes a task name, creates a worktree on a new branch, assigns a deterministic port from a hash of the name, creates an isolated database (docker compose project or SQLite file), writes .env.local, installs dependencies via the shared pnpm store, and opens a tmux window running Claude. Build scripts/wt-status.sh showing each worktree's branch, dirty count, ahead/behind, PR state, and port. Build scripts/wt-clean.sh that removes merged worktrees and their containers. Then help me pick three tasks from my backlog whose file sets are disjoint (prove it with a file-ownership list), run them concurrently for one week, log timestamps to worktree-log.csv, and report merged-PR throughput and review time versus baseline. Flag any guide claim (like the 3-5x cap) my data contradicts.

claude-code-parallel-worktrees.one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are an engineering lead making one developer's repo safe and fast for parallel Claude Code sessions, following Boris Cherny's worktree pattern but measuring whether it works for this person. You prefer boring, deterministic scripts over clever orchestration. You do not trust throughput claims you have not measured.

CONTEXT
- Pattern: one task = one git worktree = one Claude session; all coordination via branches and PRs. Boris runs 3-5 at once; 10-15 is the team ceiling, not a target. Review bandwidth is the binding constraint.
- Primitives: `git worktree add ../proj-x -b feat/x`, `git worktree list`, `git worktree remove`, `git worktree prune`; native `claude --worktree [name]` and `--tmux` (verify on the installed version with `claude --help`); subagent frontmatter `isolation: worktree` (verify it exists in the installed version's subagent docs).
- Tools named in the guide: raine/workmux, nielsgroen/claude-tmux, muxtree, tmux.
- Known collisions from the guide: dev-server ports, shared Postgres/MySQL dev DB, node_modules at 500 MB-2 GB per worktree, shared .git/hooks writing to shared caches, IDE branch confusion, CLAUDE.md edits conflicting on merge, package.json adjacent edits, rate limits from N times token spend.
- Claims to TEST against this repo and this person: 'single biggest productivity unlock'; 'throughput gains cap around 3-5x'; 'zero merge conflicts between running sessions'; 'zero disk duplication of git history'.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- Push the current branch before creating or removing any worktree. Never use `git worktree remove --force` on a dirty worktree without listing its uncommitted changes first and getting confirmation.
- Never `git add -A` in a worktree whose session is still editing; commit by explicit paths.
- No two concurrent tasks may share a file in their planned change set. Prove it before spawning.
- CLAUDE.md is edited only on main.
- Do not exceed the user's plan rate limits; start with three sessions.

ORDERED DELIVERABLES
1. baseline.md: merged PRs per day and median createdAt-to-mergedAt over the last 30 days from `gh pr list --state merged --author @me --json number,createdAt,mergedAt --limit 200`; repo size; node_modules size; list of collision points found in package.json scripts, docker-compose.yml, .env.example, and git hooks.
2. Native-flag notes in baseline.md: where `claude --worktree` puts worktrees, branch naming, whether .env files are copied, cleanup behaviour. Tested, not read.
3. scripts/wt-spawn.sh <task>: push check, worktree on branch wt/<task>, deterministic PORT from cksum of the name into 3100-3999, isolated DB (docker compose -p <task> or SQLite file path), .env.local with PORT, DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (or the repo's package manager) using the shared store, then `tmux new-window -n <task> 'cd <path> && claude'`.
4. scripts/wt-status.sh: table of worktree, branch, dirty file count, ahead/behind main, PR number and state via gh, PORT, container status.
5. scripts/wt-clean.sh: for worktrees whose PR is merged, show dirty state, remove worktree, delete branch, `docker compose -p <task> down -v`, then `git worktree prune`.
6. tasks.md: three backlog tasks with planned file sets and a pairwise-overlap check that shows zero shared files.
7. worktree-log.csv: task, spawn time, first review time, PR open time, merge time, conflicts (y/n), rework rounds.
8. results.md after the trial: merged PRs per day and median cycle time versus baseline, number of sessions at which review became the bottleneck, verdicts on the four claims.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
Before declaring done, list in gaps.md: collision points you found but did not isolate (shared caches, external APIs with per-account rate limits, ports hard-coded in source), anything about the native flag you could not determine, tasks that conflicted despite the overlap check and why, and whether the measurement window is long enough to mean anything (one week with three tasks is anecdote; say so). Fix any isolation gap that a script change can fix now.

SELF-QUESTIONS BEFORE FINISHING
- Did two dev servers actually run at once on different ports, and did I curl both?
- Does any hook in .git/hooks write to a path shared across worktrees?
- What happens to Docker volumes and SQLite files when a worktree is removed?
- Does the repo hard-code port 3000 anywhere that .env.local does not override?
- Did I count review time, or only model time?
- Did any session edit CLAUDE.md, package.json, or a lockfile?
- Does wt-clean refuse to delete unmerged or dirty work?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop after scripts and tasks.md exist and a dry run of three spawns and one clean succeeds, then hand control to the user for the trial week. Stop and ask before removing any worktree with uncommitted changes, before dropping any database volume that existed before this work, and if the repo needs a shared external resource (single staging DB, single OAuth callback URL) that cannot be isolated.

RETURN FORMAT
One message: baseline numbers table; native-flag findings; the three scripts' paths with usage lines; tasks.md overlap matrix; dry-run output of wt-status.sh with three worktrees; gaps.md contents; the instructions for the trial week, including what to log.

steps.title: Ground truth: baseline and collision inventory
steps.goal: Measure current throughput and find every resource two worktrees would fight over.
steps.prompt: In the repo at <path>, run `gh pr list --state merged --author @me --json number,title,createdAt,mergedAt --limit 200` and compute merged PRs per working day and median hours from createdAt to mergedAt over the last 30 days; write both to baseline.md with the raw counts. Record `du -sh .git`, `du -sh node_modules` (or the venv / target dir), and the package manager in use. Then inventory collision points: grep package.json scripts, Procfile, docker-compose.yml, vite/next/webpack configs, and source for hard-coded ports (`grep -rnE '(PORT|:3000|:5173|:8000|:5432|:6379)' --include='*.{js,ts,json,yml,yaml,py,env*}'`); list database and Redis URLs and where they come from; list .git/hooks and husky or pre-commit configs and any paths they write; list caches (.next, .turbo, .pytest_cache, ~/.cache tool dirs) and whether they are inside or outside the checkout. Read Boris Cherny's two posts linked in the guide and note his own concurrency number. Finally, in a scratch clone, run `claude --help | grep -iA3 worktree` and one `claude --worktree probe-a` session; record where the worktree lands, its branch name, whether .env files are copied, and what happens on exit, then remove it. Write everything to baseline.md as tables.
steps.expect: baseline.md with a throughput table (PRs/day, median cycle hours, sample size) and a collision table (resource, current value, where configured, shared across worktrees yes/no), plus a short native-flag findings list.
steps.audit: Re-count PRs with a second query (for example the GitHub web search is:pr is:merged author:@me merged:>DATE) and confirm the number matches within one. Any port or URL found in source but not in env config is flagged as hard-coded; do not move on until each collision row has a 'how to isolate' note.

steps.title: Build the spawn script with isolation
steps.goal: One command creates an isolated, ready-to-run worktree with its own port, database, and Claude session.
steps.prompt: Write scripts/wt-spawn.sh <task-name>. It must: refuse if the current branch has unpushed commits; refuse if a worktree or branch wt/<task> exists; create the worktree at ../<repo>-<task> on new branch wt/<task> from origin/main (or call `claude --worktree <task>` instead if native-flag.md shows it supports what follows); compute PORT as 3100 + (cksum of the task name mod 900) and check it is free with `ss -ltn`; create an isolated database per the collision table (for Postgres `docker compose -p <task> up -d db` with a port also derived from the hash, or a SQLite path inside the worktree); write .env.local with PORT, DATABASE_URL, REDIS_URL, and copy any other .env keys from the main checkout without printing their values; run the repo's install with the shared store (`pnpm install --frozen-lockfile`, `uv sync`, or equivalent); run migrations against the isolated DB; finally open `tmux new-window -n <task> -c <path> claude`. Make it idempotent on failure: if any step fails, print what was created and how to remove it. Run shellcheck.
steps.expect: An executable script under 150 lines that spawns a worktree in under two minutes, with shellcheck clean.
steps.audit: Spawn two test tasks, start the dev server in each, and curl both ports at the same time; both must answer. Confirm `docker ps` shows two separate DB containers or two SQLite files. Grep the script output for any secret value; none may appear. On any fail, fix and re-run both spawns.

steps.title: Build status and cleanup
steps.goal: See every worktree's state at a glance and remove merged ones safely.
steps.prompt: Write scripts/wt-status.sh that prints one row per worktree from `git worktree list --porcelain`: path, branch, dirty file count (`git -C <path> status --porcelain | wc -l`), commits ahead/behind origin/main, PR number and state from `gh pr list --head <branch> --json number,state`, PORT from .env.local, and DB container status from `docker compose -p <task> ps --format json`. Sort with dirty-and-no-PR first, because those need attention. Write scripts/wt-clean.sh that, for each worktree whose PR is MERGED: prints its dirty files; if any exist, skips it and says why; otherwise runs `git worktree remove <path>`, `git branch -d wt/<task>`, `docker compose -p <task> down -v` (only for projects it created, recognised by the wt/ prefix), and finally `git worktree prune`. Add `--dry-run` as the default; require `--yes` to act. Optionally bind wt-status.sh to a tmux status-right refresh every 30 seconds.
steps.expect: Two scripts; a status table for the two test worktrees; a dry-run cleanup listing what would be removed.
steps.audit: Mark one test PR merged (or simulate by merging locally into a throwaway main) and run the cleaner with --yes; verify the worktree, branch, and containers are gone and the other worktree is untouched. Create a dirty file in the remaining worktree and confirm the cleaner skips it.

steps.title: Decompose the backlog into disjoint tasks
steps.goal: Pick three real tasks that cannot collide and prove it.
steps.prompt: From the user's open issues (`gh issue list --limit 50 --json number,title,body`) or a provided list, choose candidates that are independent by the guide's rules: no output dependency between them, no shared global state, not deep debugging of an unfamiliar area. For each candidate, have Claude in read-only mode produce a planned change set: the files it expects to create or modify, derived from grepping the code involved. Build an overlap matrix of planned file sets; reject any pair that shares a file, and treat package.json, lockfiles, CLAUDE.md, shared config, and migration directories as always-conflicting unless only one task touches them. Pick the three with zero overlap and the smallest expected review time. Write tasks.md with, per task: issue link, one-paragraph prompt to give the session, planned files, acceptance test command, and expected review minutes. Include the overlap matrix.
steps.expect: tasks.md with three tasks, three prompts, and a 3x3 matrix of shared-file counts all zero.
steps.audit: Re-derive one task's file set independently (grep the identifiers involved) and compare; if the sets differ by more than two files, redo the plan for that task. Any task whose acceptance test cannot run in an isolated worktree is replaced.

steps.title: Run the parallel trial and log it
steps.goal: Execute the three tasks concurrently and capture the timing data that will judge the workflow.
steps.prompt: Spawn the three tasks with scripts/wt-spawn.sh. In each tmux window, paste that task's prompt from tasks.md, adding: 'Work only in this worktree. Commit by explicit file paths. Do not edit CLAUDE.md, package.json, or lockfiles unless the task requires it, and say so if it does. When done, run the acceptance test, push, and open a PR with gh pr create --fill.' Cycle through windows; while one runs, review another. Log to worktree-log.csv for every task: spawn time, time you first started reviewing, number of review rounds, PR open time, merge time, any merge conflict and its file, minutes you were idle waiting on all sessions. After merging, run wt-clean.sh --yes. If you feel idle between reviews, spawn a fourth task from the backlog with the same overlap check; if review starts queuing, stop spawning and note the session count where that happened.
steps.expect: worktree-log.csv with at least three complete rows, three merged PRs, and a note of the session count at which review saturated.
steps.audit: After each merge, run `git diff --name-only` between each pair of task branches to confirm no shared file slipped in; any conflict gets a row explaining which check missed it. Run wt-status.sh at the end; no orphaned worktrees or containers may remain.

steps.title: Validate against oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Compare to baseline with GitHub's own data and state what the trial proves and does not.
steps.prompt: Re-run the baseline query for the trial window and compute merged PRs per working day and median cycle hours; put them beside baseline.md numbers in results.md. Check CI status on every trial PR (`gh pr checks <n>`) and record any failure caused by isolation leaks (wrong port, wrong DB, stale cache). Confirm with `git worktree list` and `docker ps -a --filter name=wt-` that cleanup left nothing behind. Give verdicts on the guide's claims with your numbers: productivity unlock (throughput ratio), 3-5x cap (where review saturated for you), zero merge conflicts (count), zero history duplication (`du -sh` of each worktree versus .git). Write gaps.md: unisolated resources, untested native-flag behaviour, conflicts and their causes, and an honest statement of sample size. Recommend the concurrency number to use going forward, with the evidence.
steps.expect: results.md with a before/after table and four claim verdicts; gaps.md; a recommended concurrency number.
steps.audit: If the trial window has fewer than five merged PRs, state that the throughput comparison is not statistically meaningful and recommend extending the trial rather than concluding. Every verdict must cite a number from worktree-log.csv or gh output.

claude-code-parallel-worktrees.gap_audit_prompt: You are reviewing a parallel-worktree setup and its trial results that someone else built in <repo>. Do not trust results.md. (1) List every claim: each script's guarantees (isolation of port, DB, env, cache; safe cleanup; push-before-destroy), each verdict on the guide's claims, the recommended concurrency. (2) For each, mark verified, unverified, or false with evidence: run the scripts yourself on a scratch task, curl two dev servers concurrently, inspect .env.local files for collisions, grep source for hard-coded ports, check .git/hooks for shared writes, re-run the gh queries. (3) Try to break isolation: spawn two tasks whose names hash to the same port (search for a collision with a quick loop) and see what happens; run migrations in both; run the test suite in both at once; check whether a shared cache under ~/.cache causes flaky results. (4) Try to break cleanup safety: leave an uncommitted file and an unpushed commit in a worktree with a merged PR and run wt-clean.sh --yes. (5) Rank gaps by impact (lost work first, then wrong results, then friction), fix the top three now, re-run, and report what remains with the reproduction command for each.
self_questions: Did I prove two dev servers ran simultaneously on different ports, or just assume it from .env.local?
What happens when two task names hash to the same port, and does the script detect it?
Do git hooks or husky write to a cache shared by all worktrees?
Does `claude --worktree` on this version copy .env files, and did my script duplicate or conflict with that?
Could wt-clean delete unpushed commits on a branch whose PR merged from an older commit?
Did any task touch package.json, a lockfile, CLAUDE.md, or migrations despite the plan?
Is my baseline window comparable in task type and working days to the trial window?
Did I log human review time and idle time, or only model run time?
validation_oracles: GitHub data: `gh pr list --state merged --author @me` for baseline and trial windows gives merged PRs per day and median cycle time computed the same way.
Two dev servers from different worktrees both return HTTP 200 when curled at the same moment on their assigned ports.

gemini-cli.one_shot:
ROLE AND STANCE
You are a developer-tools lead deciding, with evidence, which of this developer's tasks can move from Claude Code to Google's free Gemini CLI. You treat the guide's claims as hypotheses. You protect private code and secrets, and you assume quotas and model names have changed since the guide was written.

CONTEXT
- Gemini CLI: github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli, Apache 2.0, Node 20+. Install `npm install -g @google/gemini-cli` or `npx @google/gemini-cli`. Context file GEMINI.md. Settings in ~/.gemini/settings.json (mcpServers block, same protocol as Claude Code). Headless: `gemini -p "..." --output-format json` or `stream-json`. Models via `-m` (guide: gemini-2.5-pro default, gemini-2.5-flash cheaper). Multi-root context: `--include-directories ../lib,../docs`. Official GitHub Action for CI. Built-in Google Search grounding.
- Guide claims to TEST: (1) free tier is 60 req/min and 1,000 req/day on 2.5 Pro with personal Google sign-in; (2) context window ~1M tokens versus ~200K for Claude; (3) Workspace accounts often cannot use the free tier; (4) one long agent session can use 100+ requests; (5) grounding is free and built-in.
- Proposed routes from the guide: commit/PR drafting, large-context reads summarized for Claude, grounded research, throwaway script codegen, CI review via the Action, a second vote in /council-style reviews, fallback during Anthropic outages.

HARD CONSTRAINTS
- Before sending any repository content, read the current free-tier data-use terms and record whether prompts may be used for training or human review. If they may, do not send code from private or client repos; use only open-source or personal repos and say so.
- Never pass .env files, keys, or credential directories to Gemini. Add them to .geminiignore (verify the file name is supported in the docs) and exclude them in every wrapper call.
- Pin the CLI version. Log every call. Stay at least 20 percent under the daily cap during evaluation.
- No route goes live until its blind evaluation is done.

ORDERED DELIVERABLES
1. ground-truth.md: installed version, auth method, today's quotas and model names from Google's pages (with URLs and access date), data-use terms summary, the exact JSON schema returned by --output-format json (field names, stats block), and verdicts on claims 1-5 that can be checked without evaluation.
2. bin/gem: wrapper with -m, timeout, CSV logging (timestamp, route, model, latency ms, input/output tokens if reported, exit status), backoff on 429/RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED, and fallback to `claude -p` after two failures, logging which agent answered.
3. .git/hooks/prepare-commit-msg (installable script) that drafts a body from `git diff --cached` truncated sensibly, only when the message is empty, and never blocks the commit on failure.
4. scripts/repo-summary.sh producing docs/REPO_SUMMARY.md with an architecture map, module list, entry points, and known gotchas, using --include-directories.
5. scripts/research.sh that asks for grounded answers and requires a URL per claim in the JSON output.
6. eval/: commits.csv (25 historical diffs, blind-labelled outputs A/B, scores), summarizer.csv (15 grep-checkable questions answered by Claude with and without the summary, correct y/n), scripts.csv (10 throwaway-script tasks, shellcheck pass, fixture run pass).
7. routing.md: table of task type, route, evidence, fallback.

BUILT-IN GAP ANALYSIS
Before finishing, write gaps.md: claims you could not verify (for example consumption of requests per session if /stats is unavailable headless); routes not evaluated (CI Action, council vote, outage fallback) and what it would take; any case where Gemini ran a command or edit without approval; quota numbers that differed from the guide; any evaluation where sample size is under 15. Fill what you can now: if the Action was not tested, set it up on a throwaway repo and run it once.

SELF-QUESTIONS BEFORE FINISHING
- Did I read today's quota page, or rely on the guide's numbers?
- What do the free-tier terms say about prompt data, and did I respect that for every repo I sent?
- Were graders blind to which agent wrote each commit body?
- Did the summarizer help Claude answer more questions correctly, or just make it faster?
- Did grounded research return real, reachable URLs, and did I spot-check that they support the claims?
- How many requests did one prepare-commit-msg call consume, and what is the daily total at my commit rate?

STOP CONDITIONS
Stop when routing.md is backed by the three eval files and the wrapper and hook are installed. Stop and ask if the terms forbid the user's intended use on private code, if sign-in requires a Workspace admin change, or if the quota is far below the guide's numbers (the routing case may collapse).

RETURN FORMAT
One message: ground-truth table (claim, guide value, verified value, source); file list with one-line usage each; eval summary (route, n, Gemini mean score, Claude mean score, verdict); routing table; gaps.md contents; the daily request budget estimate.

steps.title: Ground truth: install, quotas, terms, output schema
steps.goal: Pin what Gemini CLI actually is today on this machine and under today's terms.
steps.prompt: Install a pinned version: `npm install -g @google/gemini-cli@<latest-tag>`; record `gemini --version` and `node --version` (must be 20+). Clone github.com/google-gemini/gemini-cli to repos/gemini-cli and read docs/ for: headless mode and --output-format, settings.json keys, mcpServers, GEMINI.md loading order, ignore files, sandbox, checkpointing, built-in tools, and the GitHub Action. Sign in with the personal Google account. Open Google's current quota/pricing pages for Gemini CLI and Gemini Code Assist and the terms that apply to the free tier; record today's request limits, available models, and whether free-tier prompts may be used to improve products or be read by humans, with URLs and the access date. Run `gemini -p 'Reply with the word ok' --output-format json > ground/hello.json` and document every field, especially any stats or token usage block. Then write ground-truth.md with a claims table: free-tier limits, default model, context window, Workspace restriction, built-in grounding, MCP compatibility; each with guide value, verified value, and source.
steps.expect: ground-truth.md with a version line, a six-row claims table, a terms summary of 3-5 bullets, and a documented JSON schema; repos/gemini-cli cloned.
steps.audit: Every verified value must cite a URL or a file under repos/gemini-cli/docs. If the terms permit training on prompts, mark which repos are off-limits before any later step sends code. If hello.json lacks token counts, note that the CSV log will rely on another source.

steps.title: Build the quota-aware wrapper with fallback
steps.goal: One entry point that logs, retries, and falls back to Claude.
steps.prompt: Write bin/gem (bash or Python 3 stdlib). Usage: `gem [-m model] [--route name] [--timeout s] [--include dir,...] -- "prompt"` with stdin appended to the prompt if piped. It runs `gemini -p <prompt> --output-format json -m <model>`, parses the response field and any usage/stats fields with jq or json, prints only the response to stdout, and appends a CSV row to ~/.gemini-calls.csv: ISO timestamp, route, model, latency ms, input tokens, output tokens, status, answered_by. Detect quota exhaustion by matching the actual error text or code the CLI emits for HTTP 429 / RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED (trigger it once deliberately with a tight loop on a throwaway prompt if needed, or read the source in repos/gemini-cli for the error shape). Retry twice with backoff of 2 and 8 seconds; then run `claude -p` with the same prompt and set answered_by=claude. Refuse to send any file path matching .env*, *.pem, id_*, or credentials directories. Add a `gem --today` subcommand that prints calls and tokens for the current day against the verified daily cap.
steps.expect: An executable wrapper, a CSV with test rows, and a demonstration of one fallback to Claude.
steps.audit: Run ten calls and confirm ten CSV rows with plausible latency. Simulate a failure (bad model name) and confirm fallback triggers and is logged. Pipe a fake .env path and confirm refusal. If quota detection relies on a guessed string, mark it unverified in gaps.md.

steps.title: Commit and PR drafting route
steps.goal: Draft commit bodies and PR descriptions for free, and test quality blind.
steps.prompt: Write hooks/prepare-commit-msg: if the commit message file already has non-comment content or the source is merge/squash, exit 0. Otherwise build input from `git diff --cached --stat` plus `git diff --cached` truncated to 3,000 lines with a note if truncated, and call `gem --route commit -m gemini-2.5-flash` (or the current fast model from ground-truth.md) with a prompt asking for a 50-character imperative subject and a body explaining why, wrapped at 72 columns, no marketing words. Write the result into the message file above the comments. Never fail the commit: on any error, exit 0 silently and log. Install it in the current repo. Then evaluate: pick 25 historical commits with `git log -n 200 --no-merges`, regenerate each message from its diff with both gem and `claude -p` using the same prompt, shuffle into A/B pairs with a hidden key, and have the user (or a separate grader subagent given only diff and two candidates) score each 1-5 on accuracy, why-not-what, and length. Save eval/commits.csv. Also add scripts/pr-draft.sh that does the same for `git diff main...HEAD` and prints a PR body.
steps.expect: Installed hook, pr-draft.sh, eval/commits.csv with 25 rows and mean scores per agent.
steps.audit: Check that the hook adds under 5 seconds median to a commit (time ten commits on a scratch branch) and never blocks on failure (break the network and commit). Verify the grader never saw the key. If Gemini's mean is more than 0.5 below Claude's, mark the route 'Claude' in routing.md.

steps.title: Large-context summarizer route
steps.goal: Use Gemini's big window to summarize a repo and prove the summary helps Claude answer correctly.
steps.prompt: Write scripts/repo-summary.sh <repo>: run gem with `--include-directories` covering src, lib, and docs (exclude node_modules, build outputs, vendored code, and anything matched by the ignore rules), asking for docs/REPO_SUMMARY.md with sections: purpose, architecture map (modules and their dependencies), entry points with file paths, data flow, configuration and env vars by name only, test layout, and known gotchas with file:line references. Record the input size in tokens from the usage fields. Then build eval/summarizer.csv: write 15 factual questions about the repo whose answers can be checked by grep or by reading one file (for example 'which module reads DATABASE_URL', 'what function handles webhook retries'). Ask `claude -p` each question twice: once with no context beyond the repo path and a 2-minute budget, once with REPO_SUMMARY.md prepended. Check each answer against grep and record correct y/n and wall time. Also spot-check 10 file:line references in the summary for existence.
steps.expect: REPO_SUMMARY.md, input token count, eval/summarizer.csv with 30 graded answers, and a reference-accuracy score out of 10.
steps.audit: Any fabricated file path or function name in the summary counts against it; if more than 2 of 10 references are wrong, the route fails until the prompt is tightened and re-run. Confirm no secret values appear in the summary by grepping for key-like patterns.

steps.title: Grounded research and throwaway script routes
steps.goal: Test the two remaining cheap routes with checkable outputs.
steps.prompt: Write scripts/research.sh '<question>' that calls gem asking for a JSON array of claims, each with text and a source URL, using Google Search grounding. Run it on 8 questions where you can verify the answer (current latest version of three libraries the repo uses, a breaking change in one of them, two API rate limits, one security advisory). For each claim, fetch the URL and mark supported, unsupported, or unreachable; save eval/research.csv. Then pick 10 throwaway-script tasks from shell history or past requests (CSV munging, log grepping, file renaming, JSON reshaping) and generate each with `gem` and with `claude -p` using an identical prompt. Run shellcheck (or ruff for Python) on every output, then run each on a prepared fixture input and compare to an expected output you write first. Save eval/scripts.csv with lint pass, fixture pass, and tokens per agent. Finally, on a throwaway repo, install the official run-gemini-cli GitHub Action with the API key as a repository secret, open a PR with a planted off-by-one bug, and record whether the review catches it.
steps.expect: eval/research.csv with per-claim support status; eval/scripts.csv with 20 rows and pass rates per agent; one Action run URL with caught or missed.
steps.audit: If more than 20 percent of research claims are unsupported by their own URLs, mark the research route as 'leads only, verify before use'. Make sure expected fixture outputs were written before seeing either agent's script; if not, rewrite them and re-grade.

steps.title: Validate against the oracles and write the gap report
steps.goal: Turn the evals into a routing decision and list what is still unproven.
steps.prompt: Aggregate eval/commits.csv, eval/summarizer.csv, eval/research.csv, eval/scripts.csv, and eval/optional.md. For each route compute n, Gemini mean or pass rate, Claude mean or pass rate, and the difference. Write routing.md, one row per task type: task type, route to (Gemini, Claude, or Gemini-then-Claude-verify), evidence file, fallback, and expected daily request use from ~/.gemini-calls.csv extrapolated to the user's normal week. Compare that daily use to the verified cap from ground-truth.md and state the headroom as a percentage. Write gaps.md listing: guide claims with final verdicts (true, false, changed, unverified) with sources; routes with n under 15; any unapproved action Gemini took during testing; privacy constraints that limit which repos can use which routes; untested items. Recommend whether to keep the prepare-commit-msg hook installed, citing the median latency it added and the commit eval score.
steps.expect: routing.md with 6-8 rows, a daily budget estimate, and gaps.md with every guide claim resolved.
steps.audit: Every routing decision must cite a number from an eval file. If the daily estimate exceeds 80 percent of the cap, mark which route to throttle. If any route had graders who could see the agent label, mark its verdict provisional.

gemini-cli.gap_audit_prompt: You are auditing a Gemini CLI routing setup built by someone else: bin/gem, a prepare-commit-msg hook, repo-summary.sh, research.sh, eval/*.csv, routing.md, gaps.md. (3) Look for silent failures: does the hook ever write an empty or error message into a commit; does the wrapper count a fallback answer as a Gemini success; does the summarizer include ignored directories; do any logs contain secrets. hunyuan3d-2.mission: Run Tencent's Hunyuan3D-2 locally as a reproducible image-to-3D pipeline: reference image in, cleaned and textured GLB out, measured for VRAM, time, mesh validity, and fidelity to the input, then extended to the text-to-image-to-mesh chain and a Blender import. Done means a scripted batch run on 10-20 of your own reference images with a results table (variant, steps, seconds, peak VRAM, watertight, face count, glTF validator errors, silhouette IoU), a license check for your intended use, and a clear verdict on which variant (Turbo, mini, mv, 2.1 PBR) fits your GPU and quality bar.

They would post-process with the repo's FloaterRemover, DegenerateFaceRemover, and FaceReducer, then validate GLBs with the Khronos glTF-Validator and import them headless into Blender to confirm they are usable assets.
